Objectives This is a protocol for a Cochrane Review (intervention). The objectives are as follows: Primary objective To evaluate the benefits and harms of music‐based interventions (MBIs) for chronic pain management in adults with pain lasting more than 12 weeks, comparing MBIs with the following comparators: active care, placebo, or no treatment/waitlist control. Specifically, we aim to assess the effects of MBIs on critical outcomes, such as pain intensity, pain‐related distress, and pain interference with daily functioning. Secondary objectives To evaluate the effects of MBIs on important outcomes, including functioning and disability, psychological outcomes (e.g. depression, anxiety, pain catastrophising, kinesiophobia (fear of movement due to pain), self‐efficacy, perceived social support, wellbeing), health‐related quality of life, and sleep quality To identify and report any adverse effects associated with MBIs To examine whether intervention effects differ across prespecified subgroups (i.e. pain aetiology, type of engagement, intervention duration), using subgroup analyses where sufficient data are available status released display-pdf yes is-olf no is-manuscript no is-preprint no is-journal-matter no is-scanned no is-retracted no Collection date 2026. Background Chronic pain affects one in five adults worldwide, often leading to physical disability, emotional distress, and diminished quality of life [ 1 , 2 ]. While pharmacological treatments are the cornerstone of pain management [ 3 ], their limitations (including side effects, risks of dependency, and incomplete relief [ 4 ]) underscore the need for accessible, evidence‐based, complementary approaches [ 5 ]. Music‐based interventions (MBIs) are increasingly being studied as adjuncts in chronic pain care. These interventions seem to engage cognitive, emotional, and neurophysiological pathways that could influence pain‐related outcomes [ 6 , 7 ]. Research suggests that MBIs may be associated with changes in the descending pain modulatory system (DPMS), seemingly affecting pain perception and well‐being [ 8 , 9 ]. However, the strength and consistency of this evidence remain uncertain given the diversity in intervention types and delivery methods (e.g. self‐chosen versus prescribed music), introducing substantial heterogeneity across studies, which may affect comparability and generalisability of findings [ 10 ]. This Cochrane review will systematically evaluate randomised controlled trials (RCTs) to assess the effects of MBIs in managing chronic pain and improving associated outcomes, such as emotional well‐being, quality of life, and functional mobility. By synthesising the available evidence, identifying characteristics of effective MBIs, and testing subgroup effects, the review aims to clarify their role in chronic pain management. The resulting evidence synthesis may help inform clinical guidelines and optimise strategies for incorporating MBIs into pain care. Description of the condition Chronic pain, defined by the International Association for the Study of Pain (IASP) as pain persisting or recurring for more than 12 weeks [ 11 ], represents a leading cause of disability and reduced quality of life. It is widely conceptualised as a complex biopsychosocial condition that may involve alterations in the central and peripheral nervous systems [ 12 ]. In chronic pain, the nervous system may become increasingly sensitive to pain‐related input, a process often referred to as central sensitisation, where pain signals seem to be amplified even in the absence of ongoing tissue damage [ 12 ]. Chronic pain has also been associated with maladaptive neuroplasticity, referring to persistent changes in brain and nervous system function that may alter how pain is processed, regulated, and perceived over time [ 13 ]. In addition, the dysfunction of the DPMS, altering the regulation and inhibition of pain signals, may contribute to the persistence and emotional burden of chronic pain symptoms [ 14 ]. These neurophysiological mechanisms are thought to contribute to emotional, cognitive, and physical impairments, which may compound the overall burden on individuals and healthcare systems. Description of the intervention and how it might work MBIs are non‐pharmacological strategies that involve either receptive (e.g. music listening) [ 15 ], or active (e.g. singing, tapping, instrument playing, improvisation) engagement with music [ 16 , 17 ], delivered individually or in groups [ 18 ], and in various formats including live or recorded, self‐selected, or therapist‐provided [ 16 , 19 ]. These interventions can be administered by trained music therapists (i.e. music therapy), by healthcare professionals (i.e. music medicine), by volunteers without a therapeutic relationship (e.g. music activities), or may be self‐administered [ 20 ]. MBIs are non‐invasive and adaptable to consumer preferences, which enhances their feasibility and acceptability across diverse populations [ 21 , 22 ] ( Table 1 ). 1 Conceptual distinctions between active and receptive music‐based interventions (MBIs) Type of MBI Description Characteristics Receptive MBIs Participants focus their attention on live or recorded music, e.g. active music listening, music‐guided imagery. Participants use either self‐selected or clinician‐selected music. MBIs delivered individually or in groups. MBIs delivered by trained music therapists, healthcare professionals, or lay providers/volunteers. Interventions delivered in clinical, community, or home‐based settings, regardless of frequency or duration. Interventions described as music therapy or music medicine, provided that music is the primary and structured intervention. MBIs may be delivered in person or remotely (e.g. via digital platforms or audio recordings), and may be live or pre‐recorded. The review will exclude interventions where music is not the central focus (e.g. background music during unrelated activities). Active MBIs Participants engage in music behaviours to create music, e.g. singing, playing instruments, music improvisation, songwriting. Participants lead the musical engagement. MBIs delivered individually or in groups. MBIs delivered by trained music therapists, healthcare professionals, or lay providers/volunteers. Interventions delivered in clinical, community, or home‐based settings, regardless of frequency or duration. Interventions described as music therapy or music medicine, provided that music is the primary and structured intervention. MBIs may be delivered in person or remotely (e.g. via digital platforms or audio recordings), and may be live or pre‐recorded. The review will exclude interventions where music is not the central focus (e.g. background music during unrelated activities). Abbreviations: MBI: music‐based interventions Several mechanisms have been proposed to explain how MBIs might influence pain‐related outcomes, including potential modulation of the DPMS, engagement of emotional and reward‐related brain networks, and possible effects on cognitive and affective dimensions of pain through processes such as attention, distraction, relaxation, cognitive agency (i.e. a sense of active involvement, control, or participation in the therapeutic experience), and self‐efficacy (i.e. confidence in one’s ability to manage symptoms or cope with challenges) [ 7 , 23 , 24 , 25 ]. Neuroimaging studies have reported associations between music exposure and changes in functional connectivity and brain activation patterns [ 9 , 26 , 27 ]. To support the conceptual framework of this review, we include a logic model illustrating the hypothesised mechanisms through which MBIs may influence chronic pain outcomes ( Figure 1 ). The model integrates current evidence on chronic pain neurophysiology, including potential alterations in the DPMS, with proposed cognitive, emotional, and reward‐related mechanisms associated with MBIs. The logic model also outlines potential contextual effect modifiers, including pain aetiology, type of engagement, and intervention duration, alongside neuroimaging findings and clinically relevant outcomes. Together, this framework aims to illustrate how MBIs may influence both sensory and affective dimensions of chronic pain through interacting neurophysiological and psychosocial pathways [ 28 ]. 1 (1) Chronic pain and the descending pain modulatory system (DPMS). Chronic pain is a complex biopsychosocial condition that may involve alterations of the DPMS. Persistent activation and maladaptive plasticity may contribute to central sensitisation and facilitation, characterised by hyperexcitability in spinal and cortical neurons and potentially reduced descending inhibition from regions such as the prefrontal cortex, anterior cingulate cortex, periaqueductal gray matter, and rostral ventromedial medulla. (2) Mechanisms of action. Music‐based interventions (MBIs) may modulate pain through converging cognitive and emotional mechanisms, including attentional engagement and distraction, limbic and affective modulation, relaxation, cognitive agency (sense of control and active engagement), and self‐efficacy (confidence in managing symptoms). (3) Contextual factors. Potential effect modifiers may include the type of pain aetiology (cancer‐related pain, fibromyalgia, mixed group), type of engagement (receptive or active), and the duration of the intervention (short‐term ≤ 1 month, intermediate‐term 1 to 6 months; long‐term > 6 months). (4) Neuroimaging evidence. Neuroimaging studies suggest that MBIs may engage distributed pain‐related networks, including potential reductions in hyperconnectivity between pain‐related networks and the default mode network, which could reflect shifts in attention away from pain‐related processing such as rumination. Some studies also report increased functional coupling between limbic‐reward regions (e.g. nucleus accumbens, amygdala) and prefrontal regulatory areas. These neural changes have been associated with reductions in perceived pain intensity and emotional distress, although causal relationships remain uncertain. (5) Integration via the DPMS. By engaging cognitive‐emotional and reward‐related processes, MBIs may influence top‐down modulatory pathways of the DPMS, potentially contributing to altered nociceptive processing and modulation of central sensitisation. These interactions may be relevant for the affective and motivational dimensions of pain. (6) Clinical outcomes. Across randomised controlled trials, critical outcomes may include pain intensity (physical dimension), pain‐related distress (emotional dimension), pain‐related interference (with daily life), and adverse events. Important outcomes may include functioning and disability (mobility, physical function), psychological outcomes (depression, anxiety, pain catastrophising), quality of life, and sleep quality. Some evidence suggests that factors such as self‐selected or personalised music, repeated exposure, and active engagement, may be associated with improved outcomes; however, findings remain heterogeneous and should be interpreted with caution. The effects of MBIs may vary according to several contextual and intervention‐related factors. Clinical response may differ by underlying pain aetiology, reflecting differences in peripheral, central, and affective mechanisms of pain. Intervention effects may also depend on the type of engagement (active, receptive, or mixed), as motor involvement, attentional demands, and agency differ across formats. In behavioural and rehabilitation interventions, treatment effects can further vary according to the expertise and training of the interventionist, as therapist competence and fidelity may influence outcomes. Delivery setting (e.g. clinical, home‐based, or digital) may shape adherence, contextual support, and expectancy effects, while intervention duration may influence dose‐response relationships and sustainability of effects. Some of these factors may be considered potential effect modifiers, which we plan to examine in prespecified subgroup analyses, specifically, pain aetiology, type of engagement, and intervention duration ( Figure 1 ). Why it is important to do this review Chronic pain is one of the most challenging health issues worldwide, affecting over 20% of adults and significantly impacting physical, emotional, and economic well‐being [ 29 ]. Despite advances in pain management, many people experience inadequate relief, leading to a reliance on medications with potential risks such as dependency, side effects, and diminished quality of life [ 30 ]. This creates a critical need for alternative, non‐pharmacological strategies that are both effective and accessible [ 31 ]. MBIs represent a patient‐centred approach that aims to integrate emotional, cognitive, and sensory aspects of music alongside conventional treatments [ 32 ]. While some studies suggest potential benefits, the evidence base remains fragmented, with inconsistencies in intervention design, outcomes, and mechanisms of action [ 33 ]. This uncertainty limits the broader adoption of MBIs in clinical and policy frameworks, leaving patients and healthcare providers without clear guidance on their efficacy. This research question is particularly topical given the global focus on reducing opioid use and improving access to safe, scalable, and cost‐effective healthcare solutions [ 34 , 35 ]. MBIs may serve as a culturally adaptable and potentially empowering option for individuals and communities, especially in resource‐constrained settings [ 36 ]. For health professionals, evidence‐based MBIs may enhance therapeutic offerings, while policymakers could benefit from data supporting their inclusion in non‐pharmacological treatment guidelines [ 35 , 37 ]. No current Cochrane review addresses MBIs specifically for chronic pain; the only prior Cochrane protocol on this topic was withdrawn [ 38 ], thus leaving a gap in evidence synthesis. Objectives Primary objective To evaluate the benefits and harms of music‐based interventions (MBIs) for chronic pain management in adults with pain lasting more than 12 weeks, comparing MBIs with the following comparators: active care, placebo, or no treatment/waitlist control. Specifically, we aim to assess the effects of MBIs on critical outcomes, such as pain intensity, pain‐related distress, and pain interference with daily functioning. Secondary objectives To evaluate the effects of MBIs on important outcomes, including functioning and disability, psychological outcomes (e.g. depression, anxiety, pain catastrophising, kinesiophobia (fear of movement due to pain), self‐efficacy, perceived social support, wellbeing), health‐related quality of life, and sleep quality To identify and report any adverse effects associated with MBIs To examine whether intervention effects differ across prespecified subgroups (i.e. pain aetiology, type of engagement, intervention duration), using subgroup analyses where sufficient data are available Methods We developed the Objectives in accordance with guidance from Chapter III and Chapter 2 of the Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews of Interventions [ 39 , 40 ], ensuring that the review question is structured using the PICO framework and addresses a focused, clinically relevant topic as recommended by Cochrane standards. We will follow the Methodological Expectations for Cochrane Intervention Reviews (MECIR) when conducting the review [ 41 ], and PRISMA 2020 guidance for reporting [ 42 ], in line with guidance from Chapter 3 of the Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews of Interventions [ 43 ]. Criteria for considering studies for this review Types of studies We will include randomised controlled trials (RCTs), including parallel‐group, cluster‐randomised, and cross‐over designs that evaluate the effects of MBIs for chronic pain. Eligible studies must include a comparison group, as specified in the Objectives , and report a baseline assessment prior to the intervention and at least one follow‐up assessment after the intervention. We will include studies regardless of the setting (e.g. hospital, community, home‐based care), provided they meet the population and intervention criteria. We will exclude non‐randomised studies of interventions (NRSIs) and quasi‐randomised studies (e.g. allocation by date of birth or admission order) due to high risk of selection bias and reduced methodological reliability. We will include studies reported in full‐text, conference abstracts, or trial registry entries, provided we can obtain sufficient data to assess eligibility and extract outcome data. We will attempt to contact study authors to clarify eligibility or retrieve missing information if needed. Also, we will include unpublished data and grey literature, such as dissertations or reports, where available and relevant. We will place no restriction on the year of publication or language of the manuscript. Types of participants We will include adults with chronic pain, defined as pain persisting or recurring for more than 12 weeks, based on the IASP criteria [ 11 ]. Eligible populations will include those with primary chronic pain (e.g. fibromyalgia, musculoskeletal pain) and secondary chronic pain (e.g. cancer‐related pain, chronic neuropathic pain). We will also identify participants in terms of the subtype of pain that they have (e.g. low‐back pain, cancer‐related pain, fibromyalgia, mixed group) so we can undertake subgroup analyses. Participants with acute pain, perioperative pain, end‐of‐life palliative care, or experimental/procedural pain, will be excluded. If a study has a mixed group with different pain types, we will include the study if there are a minimum of 60% of participants with chronic pain as defined by the IASP criteria. If the study does not mention the proportion of chronic pain participants, we will contact the study authors for further clarification. We will not set any limitation on the location or setting of the participants, or demographic factors. Participants will be included regardless of age, gender, ethnicity, or socioeconomic background. We will extract details of the setting, location, age, gender, ethnicity, and socioeconomic background for each study so we can include them in planned subgroup analyses. Studies focusing on populations with co‐morbidities such as depression or anxiety will be considered if chronic pain is the primary condition. Types of interventions We will include studies that evaluate MBIs for the management of chronic pain, delivered either as standalone treatments or as adjuncts to active medical care (AC). MBIs are defined as interventions in which music constitutes the central, intentional therapeutic component, designed to reduce pain or improve pain‐related outcomes (e.g. pain‐related distress, interference, or disability). Included interventions Eligible MBIs may include the following. Receptive MBIs (e.g. music listening), where participants listen to live or recorded music, either self‐selected or therapist/clinician‐selected Active MBIs (e.g. singing, playing instruments, music improvisation, songwriting), where participants make music, through instruments, composing, or singing Interventions may be delivered as follows. Individually or in groups By trained music therapists (e.g. music therapy), other healthcare professionals, or trained facilitators (e.g. music medicine) In clinical, community, or home‐based settings In person or remotely (e.g. via digital platforms or audio recordings) Using live or recorded music We will include MBIs of any dose, duration, or intensity, provided the intervention is described with sufficient detail to allow identification of key components, including at minimum the following components. Type of engagement (receptive or active) Mode of delivery (e.g. in‐person, remote, individual, group) Session duration and frequency Music selection or stimulus characteristics (e.g. self‐selected versus prescribed, live versus recorded) If essential intervention details are missing or unclear, we will attempt to contact study authors for clarification. If we cannot obtain sufficient information to confirm eligibility, we will document this and will exclude the study. We will exclude interventions where music is used only as background or incidental (e.g. background music during an unrelated therapy), or where music is one minor component in a broader multimodal intervention (e.g. music combined with aromatherapy, massage, or combined with cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT) in the experimental arm, where it is not possible to deduce that potential effects have been driven by the music component), unless the control arm receives the same co‐interventions in the absence of the music component. Intervention grouping strategy For the primary analysis, we will pool all eligible MBIs as a single intervention category to estimate the overall effect of MBIs on chronic pain outcomes. Then, we will examine potential differences in effectiveness using prespecified subgroup analyses based on key MBI features, including the following. Pain population (e.g. low‐back pain, cancer‐related pain, fibromyalgia, mixed group) Type of engagement (receptive, active, or mixed) Intervention duration (short term ≤ 1 month, intermediate term 1 to 6 months; long term > 6 months) We will define and manage these groupings in the RevMan ‘Review criteria’ tab [ 44 ], to facilitate consistent data extraction and synthesis and to investigate potential sources of heterogeneity in treatment effects. We will base comparisons on the interventions grouped as follows. MBIs AC Placebo Comparator(s) We will investigate the effect of MBIs in addition to AC compared to AC alone. AC may include physiotherapy, pharmacological treatments, psychological therapies, or alternative complementary treatments, provided these are delivered uniformly to both the intervention and control groups. In separate analyses, we will evaluate the following comparisons. MBIs + AC versus AC alone MBIs versus no treatment or waitlist controls MBIs versus placebo We will exclude studies comparing MBIs alone versus active comparators (e.g. cognitive‐behavioural therapy or mindfulness). This approach ensures that the review assesses both the direct benefit of MBIs and the incremental benefit of MBIs when used alongside active care, while maintaining comparability across study arms and focusing on the specific contribution of the interventions. Outcome measures Chronic pain outcomes are assessed by a range of validated self‐report and clinician‐rated tools. We will include four critical outcome domains, based on a conceptual model of how MBIs may influence pain processing and daily functioning: pain intensity, pain‐related distress, pain interference, and adverse events. We will analyse each of these outcomes independently. Where studies report composite outcomes or overlapping measures, we will establish a hierarchy for inclusion in the summary of findings table. Important outcome domains will include physical functioning and disability, psychological symptoms (e.g. anxiety, depression, pain catastrophising, self‐efficacy), quality of life, and sleep quality. We will analyse psychological outcomes as separate outcome domains, rather than pooled into a composite psychological outcome. These outcomes are considered relevant for understanding the broader biopsychosocial effects of MBIs. When multiple measurement instruments are reported for the same outcome within a study, we will prioritise outcome measures according to a predefined hierarchy: (1) validated and widely used instruments with established psychometric properties in chronic pain populations; (2) instruments most frequently reported across included studies to maximise comparability; and (3) alignment with the construct definitions specified in this protocol. If more than one eligible instrument remains, we will preferentially extract the measure most closely aligned with the critical outcome domain specified in this protocol, or the measure most closely matching the conceptual outcome domain. We will categorise outcome time points as follows. T1: short term/immediate postintervention (defined as < 1 month postintervention) to detect symptom reduction of the intervention. T2: intermediate term (defined as 1 to 6 months postintervention) to detect sustained symptom reduction T3: longer term (defined as 7 to 24 months postintervention) as a measure of medium‐term to long‐term avoidance of recurrence and chronicity. We will perform subgroup analyses for one‐year to two‐year outcomes if available. If a study reports an outcome more than once during any of the above time points, we will use the latest time point within that category (e.g. if there is a measure at three months and at six months, we will use the results at six months for T2) or the time point that correlates best with other studies compared within each outcome. Critical outcomes Pain is a multidimensional experience encompassing sensory, emotional, and functional components. In this review, these domains are conceptualised as distinct but related outcomes of pain severity [ 11 , 45 ]. Accordingly, we will treat pain intensity (sensory dimension), pain‐related distress (emotional dimension), and pain‐related interference (impact on daily functioning) as separate outcomes and analyse them independently (i.e. not pooled). The critical outcomes include the following. Pain intensity : refers to the subjective perception of the magnitude of pain, typically measured using scales, such as the Visual Analog Scale (VAS) [ 46 ] or the Numeric Rating Scale (NRS) [ 47 ]. Pain‐related distress : indicates the emotional response to pain, including feelings of unpleasantness, frustration, anxiety, or helplessness caused by persistent pain. Pain‐related interference : represents the extent to which pain disrupts daily activities, such as work, social engagement, or self‐care, often assessed using tools such as the Brief Pain Inventory (BPI) [ 48 ]. Adverse events and harms : any unfavourable or unintended signs, symptoms, or experiences temporally associated with the intervention. Adverse events are considered a critical outcome to enable balanced assessment of benefits and harms, consistent with GRADE guidance for intervention evaluation [ 49 ], including non‐pharmacological interventions. We will extract the number of participants experiencing one or more adverse events, the total number of adverse events reported, and the nature and severity of events, including serious adverse events when available. Important outcomes Functioning and disability : including physical function and mobility assessed via standardised outcome measures, such as the Oswestry Disability Index (ODI) [ 50 ], or PROMIS Physical Function [ 51 ]. Psychological outcomes : including anxiety, depression, self‐efficacy, perceived support, kinesiophobia, pain catastrophising; evaluated through standardised outcome measures, such as the Beck Depression Inventory (BDI) [ 52 , 53 ], State‐Trait Anxiety Inventory (STAI) [ 54 ], Pain Self‐Efficacy Questionnaire (PSEQ) [ 55 ], Tampa Scale of Kinesiophobia [ 56 ]. Quality of life : assessed using multidimensional tools, such as the Short Form‐36 (SF‐36) [ 57 ] or EQ‐5D [ 58 ]. Sleep quality : measured using standardised outcome measures like the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI) [ 59 ]. Search methods for identification of studies We will search for all applicable studies. There will be no language exclusions for either search criteria or trial selection. We will translate non‐English language articles as needed. Our search strategy and study identification procedures will follow guidance outlined in Chapter 4 of the Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews of Interventions [ 60 ], and we will perform them in accordance with PRISMA guidance [ 42 ]. Electronic searches To identify relevant studies, we will search the following electronic databases, without restricting by date or format of publication. Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), part of The Cochrane Library PubMed (MEDLINE) Embase (Elsevier) CINAHL (EBSCO) PsycINFO (ProQuest) Web of Science (Science Citation Index Expanded, Social Sciences Citation Index, Arts and Humanities Citation Index, Conference Proceedings Citation Index – Science and Conference Proceedings Citation Index – Social Science and Humanities) Scopus (Elsevier) World Health Organization (WHO) International Clinical Trials Registry Platform (ICTRP) ( https://trialsearch.who.int/ ) ClinicalTrials.gov ( https://clinicaltrials.gov/ ) ISRCTN registry ( https://www.isrctn.com/ ) The search strategy will combine terms related to MBIs and chronic pain, using both controlled vocabulary (e.g. MeSH, EMTREE) and free‐text terms ( Supplementary material 1 ). We will apply the Cochrane Highly Sensitive Search Strategy (HSSS) to identify RCTs and exclude non‐human studies [ 61 ]. Searching other resources We will search the bibliographies of retrieved articles and relevant reviews to identify trials we may have missed, perform a citation search on ISI Web of Science to discover more recent studies, contact experts in the field, and search conference proceedings databases to identify unpublished trials. We will check the reference lists of all references cited in the reports of included studies and relevant reviews for additional eligible studies. In addition, we will contact study authors to obtain additional information where necessary. We will also consult experts in the field, such as authors of studies included in the review or researchers with expertise in the area. We will examine post‐publication amendments for all included and potentially eligible studies, including retractions, expressions of concern, errata, and corrigenda. We will do this by checking publication records in bibliographic databases, reviewing journal websites where necessary, and consulting relevant retraction databases (e.g. Retraction Watch Database). If we find that a study has been retracted or subject to serious concerns, we will exclude it or handle it according to guidance outlined in Chapter 4 of the Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews of Interventions [ 60 ], and we will document any amendments in the Cochrane review. Data collection and analysis Selection of studies Two review authors (VP‐N and CH) will independently screen the titles and abstracts of all records identified through the search strategy to assess their potential eligibility. We will obtain full‐text reports for all studies deemed potentially relevant [ 62 , 63 ]. The two review authors (VP‐N and CH) will then independently assess the full‐text articles against the inclusion criteria. Any disagreements will be resolved through discussion or, if necessary, by consulting a third review author. We will record the reasons for excluding studies after full‐text assessment using Covidence software [ 64 ], and present these in a table. We will document the selection process using a PRISMA flow diagram [ 42 ]. Multiple reports of the same study will be collated and treated as a single study, with all relevant data extracted and reported together. If we need to clarify study details to determine inclusion, we will contact the corresponding author of each study for further details. If abstracts or articles require translation into another language to determine their eligibility, we will use translation software to complete this. We will conduct and manage the study selection process through Covidence [ 64 ]. This process will follow the guidance outlined in Chapter 4 of the Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews of Interventions [ 60 , 65 ]. Several members of this review author team have published studies that may be eligible for inclusion, except CH, KJ, MR, and SK, who have not published potentially eligible studies. In accordance with Cochrane’s conflict of interest policy, detailed in Chapter 7 of the Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews of Interventions [ 66 ], the review authors involved in a given study will not participate in eligibility decisions, data extraction, risk of bias assessment, or GRADE assessments for that study. Non‐conflicted review authors will independently perform these tasks [ 43 ]. Data extraction and management Two review authors (VP‐N and CH) will independently extract data from each included study using a standardised data extraction form, developed and piloted in accordance with Chapter 5 of the Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews of Interventions [ 67 ]. If discrepancies arise, the two review authors will resolve them through discussion or by consulting a third review author if necessary. We will extract the following details. Information about data extraction from reports: names of data extractors, date of data extraction, publication's digital object identifier (DOI) Eligibility criteria: confirmation of study eligibility and conflicts of interest Where multiple reports of a single study exist, we will extract and collate data across all relevant sources. If study details are missing or unclear, we will contact study authors for clarification. We will manage references using Zotero [ 68 ], and we will manage screening and data extraction using Covidence [ 64 ]. For studies published in languages other than English, we will use translation software (e.g. Google Translate) to assess eligibility and extract relevant data. Where possible, we will seek support from fluent speakers or professional translators to verify key information. All translation procedures will be documented to ensure transparency. Where necessary, we will convert outcome data into a format suitable for meta‐analysis following the guidance in Chapter 6 of the Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews of Interventions [ 69 ]. For continuous outcomes, we will extract means and SDs; if not reported, we will calculate these from standard errors, confidence intervals (CIs), t values, or P values when possible. For dichotomous outcomes, we will extract or compute risk ratios (RRs) or odds ratios with corresponding CIs. When required data are not directly reported, we will contact study authors for clarification. All data conversions will be documented, and any assumptions clearly stated. Risk of bias assessment in included studies We will assess risk of bias in all included RCTs using the Cochrane Risk of Bias 2 (RoB 2) tool [ 70 ], as outlined in Chapter 8 of the Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews of Interventions [ 71 ]. This tool evaluates risk of bias for a specific result of a specific outcome at a specific time point, across five domains: the randomisation process, deviations from intended interventions, missing outcome data, measurement of the outcome, and selection of the reported result. We will assess risk of bias for each result based on the effect of assignment to the intervention at baseline, regardless of adherence to the intervention (i.e. the intention‐to‐treat effect). This approach reflects the pragmatic aim of determining the effect of being allocated to a music‐based intervention compared to a control. ROB 2 assessments will be conducted for outcomes contributing to the summary of findings table and GRADE assessment only (i.e. pain intensity and adverse events), prioritising the end‐of‐treatment time point. For other outcomes, we will describe the risk of bias narratively where relevant [ 72 ]. We will rate each domain as low risk of bias, some concerns, or high risk of bias, according to RoB 2 guidance. An overall risk of bias judgment will be assigned for each outcome. We will determine this using the following rules: if we rate all domains as low risk, the overall risk of bias will be low; if we have some concerns in at least one domain and none are high risk, we will rate the overall risk as some concerns; and if we rate any domain at high risk, the overall risk of bias will be high. Two review authors (VP‐N and CH) will independently assess the risk of bias for each included study. Disagreements will be resolved through discussion or by consulting a third review author. We will follow the procedures outlined in Chapter 7 and Chapter 8 of the Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews of Interventions [ 66 , 71 ]. Where necessary, we will contact study authors using the corresponding email address of the corresponding author to obtain or confirm information relevant to risk of bias assessments. RCTs will include parallel‐group, cluster‐randomised, and cross‐over designs. For cluster‐randomised and cross‐over trials, we will assess the risk of bias using RoB 2 with appropriate consideration of design‐specific signalling questions, in accordance with Chapter 23 of the Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews of Interventions [ 73 ]. No adaptations to the RoB 2 tool will be required. We will present the results of the risk‐of‐bias assessments in tabular form and through graphical visualisations using RevMan [ 44 ]. Measures of treatment effect Dichotomous data For dichotomous data, we will calculate RR with 95% CIs. Continuous data For pain outcomes measured on continuous scales, we will prioritise conversion of scores to a common metric (0 to 10 or 0 to 100, depending on the majority of included studies) and use mean differences (MDs) with 95% CIs to improve clinical interpretability. Where pain scales cannot be reliably converted to a common metric, we will use standardised mean differences (SMDs) as a secondary approach. For other continuous outcomes that cannot be meaningfully transformed to a common scale (e.g. psychological or quality‐of‐life measures using different instruments), we will use SMDs with 95% CIs. If a study provides multiple measures of the same construct, we will calculate the average effect estimate and corresponding variance across these outcomes. If a study reports both continuous and dichotomous data for the same outcome, we will convert the RR to an SMD to allow for pooling of both continuous and dichotomous data, as described in Chapter 9 of the Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews of Interventions [ 63 ]. We will interpret SMDs using standard thresholds (0.2 = small, 0.5 = moderate, 0.8 = large) unless minimally important differences are available and applicable. All planned analyses will follow the methods described in Chapter 6 of the Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews of Interventions [ 69 ], and comply with Cochrane MECIR standards [ 41 ], and PRISMA 2020 guidance [ 42 ]. Ordinal data We will analyse ordinal data as continuous data, and we will express the intervention effect as a difference in means. Unit of analysis issues The unit of analysis will be the individual participant. We will include parallel‐group, cluster‐randomised, and cross‐over randomised trials [ 74 ]. For cluster‐randomised trials, we will adjust for clustering using reported intra‐cluster correlation coefficients (ICCs) or external estimates where required. If studies report appropriately adjusted effect estimates, we will use these directly. If adjustment is not possible, we will account for clustering using the effective sample size approach, in accordance with Chapter 11 and Chapter 23 of the Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews of Interventions [ 73 , 75 ]. For cross‐over trials, we will use paired analyses where appropriate. If paired data are unavailable or if we have concerns about carryover effects, we will extract and analyse first‐period data only. For studies with more than two intervention arms, we will either combine relevant intervention groups or select a single pairwise comparison to avoid double‐counting, in accordance with Chapter 6 of the Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews of Interventions [ 69 ]. We will extract all continuous outcomes and analyse these as change‐from‐baseline scores. Where outcomes are reported at multiple time points, we will extract data closest to the end of the intervention for the primary analysis. Additional time points may be included in sensitivity or subgroup analyses. Dealing with missing data We will contact study authors to request missing outcome data or summary statistics. Where study authors do not report change‐from‐baseline scores, but baseline and post‐intervention values are available, we will calculate change scores and corresponding SDs as recommended in Chapter 6 of the Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews of Interventions [ 69 ]. If SDs or other summary statistics are missing, we will calculate them from available information (e.g. standard errors, CIs, P values), following the methods outlined in Chapter 10 of the Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews of Interventions [ 76 ]. We will not impute missing values using estimates from other studies or external sources. We will not apply methods such as ‘last observation carried forward’ or ‘best or worst case scenario imputation’ unless explicitly justified. Any such methods will be described and assessed in accordance with PRISMA 2020 guidance [ 42 ]. For dichotomous outcomes, we will conduct available‐case analysis, excluding participants with missing data, unless we can recover or validly impute outcome data. We will explore the impact of missing data through sensitivity analyses and consider their effect in the GRADE assessment of certainty. Reporting bias assessment We will assess the risk of bias due to missing results in each synthesis (arising from reporting biases) using the Risk of Bias due to Missing Evidence (ROB‐ME) tool, following guidance in Chapter 13 of the Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews of Interventions [ 77 ], and PRISMA 2020 guidance [ 42 ]. Two review authors will assess each synthesis independently. The review authors will resolve any disagreements through discussion or by consulting a third review author. We will use available trial protocols and registry entries (e.g. ClinicalTrials.gov, WHO ICTRP) to compare prespecified and reported outcomes, where available. If we suspect selective reporting, we will contact study authors to obtain or confirm missing results. For meta‐analyses including at least 10 studies, we will assess publication bias through visual inspection of funnel plots. Asymmetry will be interpreted cautiously and considered alongside the ROB‐ME assessment [ 78 ]. We will not use automation tools to assess reporting bias. All judgments will be transparently documented and considered in the GRADE assessment of certainty [ 49 ]. Synthesis methods We will conduct meta‐analyses using a random‐effects model, as we anticipate clinical and methodological heterogeneity across studies, such as differences in populations, intervention characteristics, and outcome measures [ 79 ]. This model assumes that the true effect may vary between studies. The main analyses will pool all eligible MBIs together. We will report comparisons between (1) MBIs + AC versus AC alone, (2) MBIs versus placebo, or (3) MBIs versus no treatment/waitlist controls, for each outcome. Separate meta‐analysis will be conducted for each outcome. We will analyse psychological outcomes (e.g. anxiety, depression, self‐efficacy, perceived support, kinesiophobia, pain catastrophising) as distinct outcomes, and will not combine them into a single composite psychological outcome. Separate analyses will also be conducted for pain severity, adverse events, functioning and disability, quality of life, and sleep quality. We will use subgroup analyses to look at differences between groupings of the MBIs in terms of type of pain, form of engagement, and duration. Between‐study variance (τ²) will be estimated using the restricted maximum likelihood (REML) method, which is recommended for providing accurate estimates, particularly when the number of studies is small or moderate. We will calculate CIs for the summary effect using the Hartung–Knapp–Sidik–Jonkman method, which offers more robust error estimation under heterogeneity [ 80 ]. For continuous outcomes, we will use the inverse‐variance method to calculate MDs or SMDs with 95% CIs. For dichotomous outcomes, we will use a random‐effects inverse‐variance method to calculate RRs with 95% CIs, with between‐study variance estimated using REML. For rare events or sparse data, we will consider alternative analytical approaches (e.g. generalised linear mixed models), where appropriate, potentially using software outside RevMan. This approach follows the recommendations outlined in Section 10.10.4.4 of the Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews of Interventions [ 76 ]. If meta‐analysis is not possible due to substantial heterogeneity or insufficient data, we will provide a narrative synthesis structured around intervention type, population characteristics, and outcomes. We will summarise effect estimates, direction of effect, and patterns across studies. All synthesis decisions will be transparently documented. If a study contributes multiple effect estimates to a single meta‐analysis (e.g. due to multiple outcomes or time points), we will account for statistical dependency using appropriate methods. Where feasible, we will apply robust variance estimation (RVE) to adjust standard errors. We may explore multilevel or multivariate meta‐analysis models. If dependency cannot be modelled, we will select a single estimate per study using predefined rules (e.g. prioritising primary outcomes or the longest follow‐up). We will assess heterogeneity using a combination of visual inspection of forest plots, and the I² statistic [ 81 ], to quantify inconsistency, tau‐squared (τ²), to estimate between‐study variance, and 95% prediction intervals, where appropriate, to indicate the expected range of effects in similar future studies. Heterogeneity will be interpreted in the context of clinical and methodological diversity, and explored through subgroup and sensitivity analyses where applicable. We will conduct meta‐analyses using RevMan where possible [ 44 ]. For advanced models (e.g. RVE or multilevel meta‐analysis), we will use R (e.g. meta, metafor, robumeta packages) [ 82 ]. Investigation of heterogeneity and subgroup analysis We anticipate substantial clinical and methodological heterogeneity across studies, due to differences in populations, interventions, delivery formats, outcome measures, and study design. In line with Chapter 10 of the Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews of Interventions [ 76 ], we will investigate potential sources of heterogeneity using subgroup analyses. We plan to conduct three subgroup analyses, where sufficient data are available (i.e. at least 10 studies per comparison). These will be based on study‐level variables, with each study contributing to only one category per subgroup. All subgroup analyses are pre‐specified and will be treated as exploratory, recognising that they are observational in nature and may be affected by confounding and ecological bias. We will not interpret subgroup differences based on within‐subgroup significance levels, as this approach is misleading and discouraged by Cochrane guidance. First, we will explore differences in effectiveness by pain conditions. Subgroups will include: (1) musculoskeletal pain; (2) neuropathic pain; (3) fibromyalgia or other central sensitisation conditions; (4) cancer‐related pain; and (5) mixed aetiology, to classify studies that include participants with multiple types of pain. We will explore whether effectiveness varies by underlying pain mechanism. Second, we will assess the type of participant engagement, distinguishing between (1) active MBIs that require musical behaviours (e.g. singing, playing instruments, composing, dancing); (2) receptive MBIs that involve listening; and (3) mixed forms of engagement. We hypothesise that mixed interventions may be most effective, as they may enhance flexibility and accessibility while retaining therapeutic supervision. Third, we will examine intervention duration. We will categorise interventions as short‐term (≤ 1 month), medium‐term (1 to 6 months), or long‐term (> 6 months). We expect that longer interventions may produce more sustained effects, though adherence and treatment fatigue may moderate outcomes. Where feasible, we will test subgroup differences using interaction tests in RevMan [ 44 ], based on a random‐effects model. This approach aligns with Section 10.11.4 of the Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews of Interventions [ 76 ], which recommends random‐effects models for subgroup comparisons due to the increased risk of false positives under fixed‐effect assumptions [ 83 ]. We will report P values for interaction and I² values for subgroup differences, where available. Subgroup comparisons will only be made where subgroups are independent and mutually exclusive. If meta‐analysis is not feasible, we will conduct a structured narrative synthesis, grouping studies by key characteristics and examining patterns in direction and size of effect, using structured tables. All deviations from the planned analyses will be transparently reported in the review. Equity‐related assessment We will consider health inequities in this review, following guidance in Chapter 16 of the Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews of Interventions [ 84 ]. We will use the PROGRESS‐Plus framework to identify and assess populations that may experience disadvantage with respect to chronic pain and access to or benefit from MBIs [ 85 ]. This includes, but is not limited to, differences by place of residence, race/ethnicity, occupation, gender/sex, education, socioeconomic status, and additional factors such as age, disability, and stigma. During data extraction, we will collect equity‐relevant characteristics of participants and settings (e.g. low‐ and middle‐income countries versus high‐income countries; socio‐economic status of participants) and report these in the ‘Characteristics of included studies’ section. Where subgroup data are available, we will consider conducting subgroup analyses or narrative comparisons. We will document methodological decisions that affect equity considerations, including inclusion/exclusion criteria, outcome selection, and planned subgroup analyses. If available, we will draw on evidence describing lived experiences of relevant populations (e.g. racism, stigma, access barriers) to inform interpretation. These procedures may be elaborated in a supplementary file on equity methods. We may consult guidance from the PRO EDI initiative to support integration of equity, diversity, and inclusion principles [ 86 ], acknowledging that this resource is still in development and not formally endorsed by Cochrane. Sensitivity analysis Risk of bias : we will conduct sensitivity analyses to determine the impact of risk of bias on the results of meta‐analyses by excluding trials rated as being at high risk of bias arising from the randomisation process (random sequence generation and allocation concealment), deviations from intended interventions (performance bias), and measurement of the outcome (blinding of outcome assessment), as recommended in Chapter 13 of the Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews of Interventions [ 77 ]. In the context of MBIs for chronic pain management, selection bias (due to lack of randomisation and concealment), performance bias (due to lack of blinding of participants and personnel), and detection bias (due to lack of blinding in outcome assessment) may have a more substantial impact on the reliability of the results compared to attrition or reporting bias. Choice of meta‐analysis model : we will assess the possible impact of random‐effects models on inflated effect sizes, which may arise when a number of small studies are included, by repeating our analyses using a fixed‐effect model as described in Synthesis methods above. Intervention reporting: where applicable, we will conduct sensitivity analyses excluding studies with incomplete or poorly reported intervention descriptions to assess the robustness of findings to reporting quality. Missing data : where sufficient data are available, we will conduct sensitivity analyses to examine the impact of missing outcome data (e.g. complete‐case versus available‐case analyses, or exclusion of studies with substantial missing data), consistent with the approach we describe in the Dealing with missing data section. Certainty of the evidence assessment We will present a summary of findings table to summarise the effects of MBIs for chronic pain management based on evidence from RCTs. We will use the procedure described by Schünemann and colleagues [ 87 ]. The key findings from the review will include the quantity of data, magnitude of effect size, and overall certainty of the evidence. Our summary of findings table will include the measurement most often used for pain intensity and adverse events. We will prioritise the following comparisons for presentation in the formal summary of findings table, as these are most relevant for decision‐making: (1) MBIs + AC versus AC alone, (2) MBIs versus placebo, or (3) MBIs versus no treatment/waitlist controls. We will present the end‐of‐treatment results. Two review authors (VP‐N and CH) will assess the certainty of evidence using the GRADE approach across domains of study limitations, publication bias, imprecision of results, inconsistency of results, and indirectness of evidence [ 88 ]. We will categorise our overall judgement regarding the certainty of the evidence as either high, moderate, low, or very low. We will resolve any disagreements by discussion with a third review author. Consumer involvement Where feasible, we will invite one or more consumers (e.g. people with lived experience of chronic pain) to assess the Plain Language Summary and provide feedback on clarity, readability, and relevance.
