There were some concerns about the risk of bias on elements in all but two of the included studies [ 39 , 40 ]. Most risk of bias was related to the selection of the reported results not being verifiable due to a lack of pre-published study protocols [ 36 , 38 , 41 – 43 ]. Two studies did not describe whether allocation to a treatment was concealed until participants were enrolled [ 38 , 42 ] and two studies did not describe the handling of missing data [ 38 , 43 ]. An overview of the risk of bias assessment is provided in Fig. 2 . Fig. 2 Risk of bias as assessed with the revised Cochrane Risk of Bias tool Results of individual studies All studies reported improvement in pain and disability in both the exercise and placebo groups. Three studies reported no significant differences in outcome between exercise and placebo treatment [ 36 , 41 , 43 ]. Five studies reported small significant differences in outcome between exercise and placebo treatment [ 37 – 40 , 42 ]. The results of the individual studies are presented in Table 1 . Meta -analysis One study could not be included in the meta-analysis due to missing outcome information [ 43 ]. The PCE was calculated both for the individual study results and for the pooled results. The PCE per study ranged from 0.17 to 1.05. The pooled standardized mean difference of exercise therapy was 1.15 for pain (95% CI 0.57 to 1.74) and 0.55 (95% CI 0.28 to 0.82) for disability. The pooled PCE of exercise therapy was 0.60 (95% CI 0.40–0.89) for pain and 0.69 (95% CI 0.48–1.00) for disability. Forest plots of the PCE for both pain and disability are presented in Fig. 3 A and B. Fig. 3 A Proportion attributable to the contextual effect for pain. B Proportion attributable to the contextual effect for disability For pain, the statistical heterogeneity of the PCE was statistically significant with p = 0.04 and I 2 = 59.21%. For disability, the statistical heterogeneity of the PCE was not statistically significant with p = 0.70 and I 2 = 0%. Assessment of the body of evidence (GRADE) The certainty of the evidence was assessed with the GRADE method and is considered to be low. The results of the GRADE assessment are presented in Table 2 . Table 2 Results of GRADE assessment Certainty assessment Summary results Number of participants (studies) Risk of bias Inconsistency Indirectness Imprecision Publication bias Overall certainty of evidence Number of participants Exercise Placebo Effects Pain: 233 (8 RCTs) Not serious Serious a Serious b Not serious Not serious ⨁⨁◯◯ Low 495 504 PCE 0.60 (95% CI 0.40–0.89) Disability: 233 (4 RCTs) Not serious Serious a Serious b Not serious Not serious ⨁⨁◯◯ Low 236 238 PCE 0.69 (95% CI 0.48–1.00) a I 2 Greater than 40% b Exercise and placebo interventions differed between RCTs Discussion The aim of this systematic review and meta-analysis was to investigate the proportion of pain and disability improvement attributable to contextual effects in exercise therapy for patients with low back pain. The PCE of the pooled effect size was 0.60 for pain and 0.69 for disability. This means that 60% of the pain reduction and 69% of disability reduction after exercise therapy for low back pain can be explained by contextual effects. For the interpretation of the magnitude of these PCEs, one should keep in mind that the effects reported for exercise therapy in low back pain are small and that their clinical importance can be disputed (4). Sixty or 69% of a small effect is a small effect. Furthermore, the certainty of evidence we found was low which implies that the true effect might be markedly different from the effect estimated in our review. A major strength of the present review is, that it assesses the magnitude of the contextual effect as part of exercise therapy in a head-to-head comparison by calculating a ratio. Two other systematic reviews took a different approach and compared placebo treatment to no treatment in low back pain. A review by Strijkers et al. included RCTs and another review by Van Lennep et al. included both RCTs and experimental studies in low back pain [ 19 , 44 ]. Both meta-analyses reported positive significant short-term effects of placebo treatments versus no treatment in chronic low back pain [ 19 , 44 ]. A recently published systematic review included only three-arm RCTs comparing the effects of conservative, mainly passive, interventions versus placebo interventions versus no interventions in chronic low back pain. On average, participants allocated to all three groups improved in pain and function but the largest improvements were attributable to changes observed with no treatment [ 18 ]. Another systematic review and narrative synthesis by Sherriff et al. focused on intervention studies in low back pain, not limited to RCTs, that specifically manipulated certain contextual factors such as patient beliefs and patient-practitioner relationships. Overall, positive effects were found for pain and physical functioning, although the lack of a meta-analysis limited the interpretation of the results [ 45 ]. Our findings are comparable to those of the meta-analysis by Zou et al. and the meta-analysis by Whiteside et al., both of which investigated the PCE in pain populations. Zou et al. found a PCE of 0.75 for osteoarthritis pain treatments and Whiteside et al. found a PCE of 0.60 for fibromyalgia pain treatment [ 22 , 23 ]. Both systematic reviews included RCTs on pharmacological and non-pharmacological treatments in their calculation of the PCE. The PCE for exercise treatment in low back pain has never been investigated and our study shows that similar proportions apply to this population. The type of exercises and placebo treatments differed between studies, although the duration and number of sessions for the intervention and placebo arms were held constant within the studies. The two crossover studies included only one intervention session, whereas the other study included between six and twelve sessions [ 38 , 42 ]. Our analysis approach for the two randomized cross-over trials, to collect all measurements from the intervention and control periods as if the trial were a parallel group trial, is simple and most feasible given the data usually presented in publications. However, it is generally not recommended and can therefore be seen as a limitation [ 28 ]. On the other hand, this approach is considered conservative and is likely to result in wider confidence intervals and under- rather than over-weighting of trials [ 28 ]. We therefore considered it defensible in the context of our review. We performed additional analyses excluding the two crossover studies, but the heterogeneity and PCE remained approximately the same (data not shown). The large confidence interval for the PCE in the study by Preyde et al. [ 41 ] was caused by the small mean difference between the baseline and follow-up measurement in that study. This small difference is used to calculate the standard error of the PCE with the delta method, which results in an inflated but correct value and consequently a large value for the confidence interval. Furthermore, there was some heterogeneity between study populations because we included all patients with low back pain regardless of the duration of symptoms. However, we performed a further analysis of possible differences in outcomes between patients with acute low back pain (< 3 months duration) and chronic low back pain (> 3 months duration) [ 46 ]. This PCE for both pain and disability remained similar with 0.64 (95% CI 0.48–0.85) for pain and 0.68 (95% CI 0.45–1.02) for disability, indicating that longer duration of low back pain did not lead to lower PCEs. The type of placebo interventions used in the included studies could be a limitation because they do not meet many of the current recommendations for control interventions as described by the Control Interventions in Efficacy Trials of Physical, Psychological, and Self-Management Therapies (CoPPS) statement [ 47 ]. The majority of studies used sham devices in their placebo treatments, while these treatments should ideally be structurally equivalent to active treatments as much as possible. This is, of course, difficult to achieve in exercise interventions for the obvious reasons. Initiatives such as the Tidier-placebo checklist and the CoPPS statement will help researchers to improve the design, conduct, and reporting of control interventions in this field [ 47 , 48 ]. In order to make a valid comparison between an active intervention and a placebo treatment in an RCT, the expectations regarding the effects of the treatment (i.e., the credibility of the treatment) should be similar in both groups. Only two of the included RCTs measured credibility prior to the start of the intervention. They found no differences in treatment credibility between the groups prior to the start of the intervention [ 37 , 39 ]. Publication bias may occur when studies with less favorable outcomes are less likely to be published. We did not assess publication bias with the funnel plot and Egger’s test because fewer than ten studies were included in the meta-analysis. However, less favorable outcomes in research usually mean a small difference between the placebo treatment and the real treatment, so it is not unlikely that these unpublished studies would have increased the PCE. There was a risk of bias in the studies that were included, but this was not our main concern. Figure 2 shows that the most common shortcomings were related to the selection of reported results. They were not verifiable due to a lack of pre-published study protocols. The majority of studies were however published at a time when this was not common practice. In addition to the risk of bias, there were other concerns, as reported above, that led us to downgrade the certainty of the evidence. In the introduction, it was hypothesized that contextual effects may account for a large proportion of the reduction in pain and disability following exercise therapy for low back pain. The results of our meta-analyses support this hypothesis although the certainty of evidence is still low. It is important for researchers and clinicians to realize that contextual effects are an important part of the treatment effect. These contextual effects can be optimized to enhance treatment outcomes [ 49 ]. A study by Rossettini et al. showed that 52% of physical therapists surveyed already use contextual effects to enhance treatment outcomes by improving the empathetic therapeutic alliance, adopting a patient-centered approach and positive verbal communication [ 50 ]. It is important that future studies focus on identifying important contextual factors, to assess whether they are being adequately used by clinicians, and on finding ways for clinicians to influence and optimize them. Improving contextual care could enhance treatment outcomes, which would reduce the global burden of low back pain. It would be helpful if future RCTs comparing active and placebo interventions report PCE as well as overall treatment effects to gain insight into the magnitude of contextual effects in low back pain care. It is also necessary that placebo-controlled intervention RCTs adhere to the CoPPS guidelines as much as possible [ 47 ]. Conclusions A substantial part of pain and disability improvement after exercise therapy in low back pain is attributable to contextual effects. It should be noted however that this conclusion is based on low certainty evidence indicating that the true effect may differ noticeably from the effect estimated in our review. documents.title: Prevalence and clinical patterns of urolithiasis in sub-saharan Africa: a systematic review and meta-analysis of observational studies.
documents.abstract:
BACKGROUND AND OBJECTIVE: Urolithiasis, the presence of stones in the urinary tract, has been linked to various clinical features and reported as a worldwide health concern. Its prevalence varies across different regions as well as populations. Several primary studies have been conducted in Sub-Saharan Africa on the situation. However, their reports are inconsistent. Hence, this review aimed to assess the pooled magnitude of urolithiasis and its clinical patterns among hospital-visiting patients in sub-Saharan Africa.
METHODS: Online databases such as PubMed, Hinari, the African Journals online database, and Google Scholar were used to comprehensively search articles published until June 28, 2023, about the prevalence and clinical patterns of urolithiasis in Sub-Saharan Africa. All the included studies were conducted at hospital setting. The retrieved data was exported to STATA version 16 for final analysis. A random-effect meta-analysis model was computed to estimate the pooled results. The heterogeneity of the studies was assessed using I2 and Cochran's Q. Publication bias was examined by observation using funnel plots and statistically by Egger's tests. Subgroup analysis was performed based on the country where the studies have been conducted.
RESULT: A total of 26 articles (11 reported both prevalence and clinical pattern, 5 reported only prevalence, and 10 reported only clinical patterns of urolithiasis) were included in the final systematic review and meta-analysis. The pooled prevalence of urolithiasis among hospital-visiting patients was 9.4% (95% CL = 4.9-14%), with significant heterogeneity. Most of the urolithiasis was located in the kidney, with an estimated pooled proportion of 4.6% (95% CI = 2.7, 6.5), followed by bladder stone-2.0% (95% CI = 0.7, 3.4), ureteral stone-1.8% (95% CI = 0.7, 2.9), and urethral stone-0.2% (95% CI = 0.00, 0.05). The subgroup analysis showed the highest prevalence of urolithiasis was found in Mauritian, 28.1% (95%CI 24.5, 31.7), followed by Ethiopia 18.1%, and the lowest was in Eritrea, 1.0%. A sensitivity analysis using the random-effects model found no influential study on the pooled prevalence of urolithiasis. Evidence of significant publication bias was observed and trim-fill analysis was conducted for adjustment. Accordingly, two missing studies were identified, and after adjustment, the combined prevalence of urolithiasis was estimated to be 10.7%. The study also found that urolithiasis prevalence per gender was 6.3% in males and 2.9% in females. The most common clinical presentation of urolithiasis was flank pain at 58.4% (95% CL=, 45.9, 70.8), followed by low back pain at 45.9% (95% CL=, 23.1, 68.8), and nausea/vomiting at 29.9% (95% CI: 1 1.1, 48.8).
CONCLUSION: The prevalence of urolithiasis in Sub-Sahara African Countries is increasing even though a remarkable regional variation was observed, with higher predominance in males than females. Common clinical presentations of urolithiasis were flank pain, low back pain, and nausea/vomiting.

Background and objective Urolithiasis, the presence of stones in the urinary tract, has been linked to various clinical features and reported as a worldwide health concern. Its prevalence varies across different regions as well as populations. Several primary studies have been conducted in Sub-Saharan Africa on the situation. However, their reports are inconsistent. Hence, this review aimed to assess the pooled magnitude of urolithiasis and its clinical patterns among hospital-visiting patients in sub-Saharan Africa. Methods Online databases such as PubMed, Hinari, the African Journals online database, and Google Scholar were used to comprehensively search articles published until June 28, 2023, about the prevalence and clinical patterns of urolithiasis in Sub-Saharan Africa. All the included studies were conducted at hospital setting. The retrieved data was exported to STATA version 16 for final analysis. A random-effect meta-analysis model was computed to estimate the pooled results. The heterogeneity of the studies was assessed using I 2 and Cochran’s Q. Publication bias was examined by observation using funnel plots and statistically by Egger’s tests. Subgroup analysis was performed based on the country where the studies have been conducted. Result A total of 26 articles (11 reported both prevalence and clinical pattern, 5 reported only prevalence, and 10 reported only clinical patterns of urolithiasis) were included in the final systematic review and meta-analysis. The pooled prevalence of urolithiasis among hospital-visiting patients was 9.4% (95% CL = 4.9–14%), with significant heterogeneity. The subgroup analysis showed the highest prevalence of urolithiasis was found in Mauritian, 28.1% (95%CI 24.5, 31.7), followed by Ethiopia 18.1%, and the lowest was in Eritrea, 1.0%. A sensitivity analysis using the random-effects model found no influential study on the pooled prevalence of urolithiasis. Evidence of significant publication bias was observed and trim-fill analysis was conducted for adjustment. Accordingly, two missing studies were identified, and after adjustment, the combined prevalence of urolithiasis was estimated to be 10.7%. This includes cystolithiasis (bladder stone, bladder calculi), ureterolithiasis (ureteral stone), urethrolithiasis (urethral calculi) [ 1 , 3 ] and stones of the renal pelvis as well as the calyces [ 4 ]. The stone is mostly logged in the kidney and is a common urinary tract disorder [ 5 ]. Although it is a multifactorial disorder, the main cause of urinary stones is the deposition of calcium, phosphates, and oxalates in the urinary tracts, which pose serious health risks [ 6 ]. While the pathophysiologic mechanism of stone formation is a complex biochemical process, the condition occurs when stone crystals supersaturate the urine and begin to crystallize, commonly within the renal parenchyma [ 7 , 8 ]. These crystals will aggregate together and continue to enlarge with the potential to migrate into the descending urinary tract area [ 7 ]. Irrespective of the stone type, patients appear with a similar spectrum of symptoms, ranging from asymptomatic to critically ill. These symptoms can include abdominal or flank pain that comes and goes, blood in the urine (usually only visible under a microscope), nausea, vomiting, and fever [ 9 ]. If not treated early, it may result in urinary obstruction, infection, and renal failure [ 10 , 11 ]. Though approximately 90% of stones are spontaneously passed out of the urinary tract, the remaining stones generally require surgical interventions like ureteroscopy percutaneous nephrolithotomy, or non-invasive shock wave lithotripsy [ 12 ]. The epidemiology of urolithiasis varied across populations and regions and ranged from 8.8% in North America between 2007 and 2010 [ 13 ], 5–10% in Europe in the decay before 2011 [ 14 ], and 1–5% in Asia [ 15 ]. Globally, the incidence is thought to be between 1% and 5%, with affluent countries having a higher prevalence (2–13%) than developing ones (0.5–1%) [ 15 , 16 ]. This regional difference may be due to a variation of determinants such as climate, diet, fluid intake, genetics, gender, occupation, and age, which all can be potential factors for epidemiological variation [ 17 ]. Although it is more common in Afro-Asian stone-forming nations, it is becoming more common in tropical and sub-Saharan African countries as a result of rising global temperatures and rising socioeconomic status, which is demonstrated by a more Westernized food and way of life [ 15 , 17 , 18 ]. The epidemiology of urolithiasis in the majority of Sub-Saharan Africa has been poorly studied since the estimation is often based on the number of hospital admissions, which may not accurately reflect the true incidence and prevalence in the general population [ 16 , 19 ]. However, recent studies have shown a rise in the prevalence and incidence of urolithiasis in the area, even though there is an inconsistent report [ 2 , 15 , 20 , 21 ]. Moreover, and to the extent of our search, the situation in the region has not been systematically assessed yet. Therefore, this review is intended to assess the pooled prevalence of urolithiasis and its clinical pattern among hospital-visiting patients in SSA. Significance of the study This systematic review and meta-analysis study may fill data gaps, inform public health strategies, enhance clinical practice, and guide future research in SSA. It could help to address inconsistencies in reports across individual studies, providing a clearer understanding of the disease burden. It highlights regional variations and informs public health policies for targeted interventions. Understanding clinical patterns, such as common symptoms, and complications, can improve clinical practice and patient management, especially in regions with limited diagnostic facilities. In addition, the finding of this study supports the health research community by providing a comprehensive overview of the disease burden in a region often underrepresented in global health studies. Furthermore, the findings can identify gaps in existing literature, ensuring future research addressing issues related to urolithiasis in SSA. Methods Search strategy The Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analysis (PRISMA) standards were followed when executing the search techniques [ 22 ] (Supplementary File 1). The protocol was registered by the International Prospective Register of Systematic Reviews (PROSPERO) with registration number [CRD42023440816]. Online databases such as PubMed, Hinari, African Journals online database, and Google Scholar were used to comprehensively search articles published until June 28, 2023. The databases were searched by combining different MeSH terms and keywords, using Boolean Operator (OR, AND) (Supplementary File 2). For example for PubMed, the following search strategy were entered (((((Prevalence[Title/Abstract]))) AND ((Urolithiasis[Title/Abstract] OR “Urinary Lithiasis“[Title/Abstract] OR “Lithiasis, Urinary“[Title/Abstract] OR “Urinary Calculi” OR” Urinary Tract Stone“[Title/Abstract] OR “Urinary Stones“[Title/Abstract] OR “Urinary Stone“[Title/Abstract])) AND ((“Risk Factor” [Title/Abstract] OR “associated factors“[Title/Abstract] OR “determinants“[Title/Abstract]))) AND ((“Country name “[Title/Abstract])). To make sure that all pertinent studies carried out in the field are found, we also looked over the reference lists of the included studies. In addition, a manual search and a review of grey literature were used to find unindexed research publications. Eligibility criteria We used the CoCoPop approach (condition, context, and population), which is used for systematic reviews of prevalence studies, to define the criteria for including and excluding studies [ 23 ]. According to this approach, the original full-text studies that looked at the clinical patterns and prevalence of urolithiasis within a particular time, target population, and geographic area were included. Following a careful review of the articles’ content, studies that satisfied the following requirements were included. Study participants (Population): adults. Types of studies: observational studies. The outcome of interests (Condition): studies reported the prevalence and/or clinical characteristics of urolithiasis. Publication condition: All published articles and gray literature, master thesis, and dissertations. Language: English language. Publication setting (Context): studies conducted in SSA before June 28, 2023. Hence, observational studies that reported the prevalence and/or clinical characteristics of urolithiasis among adult patients visiting hospitals in SSA were included. Whereas, studies published in languages other than English reviews, editorial opinions, case reports, letters to the editor, hypotheses, and abstracts from conferences were excluded. Data extraction Two investigators (AB and MB) independently assessed the eligibility of articles and extracted data using Microsoft Excel. Using a standardized data extraction form, the following data elements were extracted from each article. Author name, Study area, Publication year, Study design, Sample size, proportion of stone, type of stone, anatomical location of stone, means of diagnosis, and proportion of each clinical pattern. Any disagreement between the reviewers was resolved by discussion. Quality assessment To evaluate the methodological quality of the included studies, the Joanna Briggs Institute’s critical appraisal tool (JBI) for observational studies was utilized [ 24 ]. Studies with an average quality score of ≥ 50% were considered to be of good quality and hence included for analysis (Supplementary file 3). Data synthesis and analysis The retrieved data was exported to STATA version 16 for final analysis. The data were presented using narrative synthesis, and tables and figures were used to display the results. The combined effect sizes of urolithiasis, accompanied by a corresponding 95% CI were calculated using the random-effect meta-analysis model. Publication bias was examined by observation using funnel plots and statistically by Egger’s tests. The trim-and-fill analysis was then done in the asymmetrical funnel plots to integrate missing studies and provide the reliability of the effect size estimate about publication bias. We also assessed heterogeneity by using Cochran’s Q test and I 2 test statistics. A p-value of < 0.05 for the I 2 test was used to determine the presence of heterogeneity. A pre-defined subgroup analysis was performed based on the country where the studies were conducted to identify the source of heterogeneity. Moreover, sensitivity analysis was performed to investigate the stability or robustness of the pooled estimates to outliers and the impact of individual studies using a leaf-one-out approach. Outcome of interest The primary outcome of this study was the pooled prevalence of urinary tract stones, which was reported in the original paper as a percentage and/or as the number of patients with urolithiasis per total number of participants. The secondary outcome was the combined clinical patterns of and anatomical location of urinary stones. Results Study selection A total of 240 articles were identified from online electronic database searching, PubMed (n = 102), Google Scholar (n = 111), Hinari (n = 13), and African Journals online database (n = 20). The title, abstract, and full text of the article were evaluated. Out of them, 57 articles were excluded due to duplication, 45 articles that had unrelated titles and abstracts were excluded since they had nothing to do with the topic in question, and 112 articles were excluded for not having other required data. 4 papers were found by cross-references of the included studies. Finally, 16 eligible articles were selected for the final systematic review and meta-analysis of the prevalence of urolithiasis, and 21 articles for clinical patterns of urolithiasis (Fig. 1 ). Fig. 1 Flow chart of study selection for systematic review and meta-analysis of the prevalence and clinical patterns of urolithiasis among hospital-visiting patients in Sub-Saharan Africa, 2023) Characteristics of the included studies A total of 26 articles (11 reported both prevalence and clinical pattern, 5 = reported only prevalence, 10 = reported only clinical patterns of urolithiasis) were included in the final systematic review and metanalysis (Tables 1 and 2 ). All studies followed a hospital-based cross-sectional study design. A total of 95,922 participants were represented in the prevalence of urolithiasis and clinical patterns of urolithiasis were reported for 2709 urolithiasis cases. All the studies were published from 2010 to 2023 in different Sab-Saharan African Countries. Of the studies reporting the prevalence of urolithiasis, three studies were conducted in Ethiopia [ 25 – 27 ], and three studies were in Congo Brazzaville [ 21 , 28 , 29 ]. The total number of participants per study ranged from 140 to 32,370. (Table 1 ). Clinical patterns of urolithiasis We analyzed the proportion of eleven clinical presentations of urolithiasis in 21 studies involving 2709 patients. Accordingly, flank pain at 58.4% (98% CL=, 45.9, 70.8), followed by low back pain at 45.9% (98% CL=, 23.1, 68.8), and nausea/vomiting at 29.9% (95% CI: 1 1.1, 48.8)0.61.8) were found to be the most common clinical patterns of urolithiasis (Table 4 ). Even though the epidemiology and clinical presentations of urinary tract stones have been thoroughly investigated in many different regions of the globe, it is largely unknown in SSA till a few years ago. However, current individual studies have shown the rise in prevalence and incidence of urolithiasis in the region, while there is an inconsistent report [ 2 , 15 , 20 , 21 ]. Therefore, this systematic review and meta-analysis aimed to assess the combined prevalence and clinical patterns of urinary tract stones among hospital-visiting patients in the SSA countries. We compressively analyzed the prevalence of urolithiasis in 16 studies involving 95,922 participants. Accordingly, the hospital pooled prevalence of urolithiasis in this study was found to be 9.4% (95% CL 4.9–14.0). The finding was in line with the previous meta-analyses that reported the overall prevalence of urolithiasis in China (8.1%) [ 50 ], in the USA ( 8.8%) [ 51 ] and Iran (6.6%) [ 52 ]. This evidence of the increasing prevalence of urolithiasis in the region may be due to changes in lifestyle and dietary patterns (a more Westernized food and way of life). However, the combined prevalence was lower than a study reported in Russia (35.4%) [ 53 ]. This may be possibly due to the difference in healthcare access, the inaccessibility of advanced modern imaging techniques like urologic CT scans [ 54 ], and the variability of lithogenic factors including environmental, genetics, and dietary habits [ 55 , 56 ]. For example, in terms of healthcare infrastructure and its capacity to manage urolithiasis, most SSA regions have limited access to advanced diagnostic tools like CT scans [ 57 , 58 ], which results in the underreporting of smaller or asymptomatic and radiolucent stones. Treatment options are also constrained by a shortage of specialized healthcare providers and facilities, leading to a reliance on symptomatic management [ 58 ]. Additionally, healthcare resources in SSA are often focused on infectious diseases, reducing resources for chronic non-communicable conditions like urolithiasis, and underdiagnosis is often due to limited access to facilities [ 59 ]. Hence these reasons might be responsible for the discrepancy. We also evaluate the prevalence of urinary calculi based on the anatomical location. The finding showed a higher combined prevalence of renal stone-4.6% (95% CI = 2.7, 6.5), followed by bladder stone-2.0% (95% CI = 0.7, 3.4). Our results are similar to previous studies [ 50 ], which reports kidney is the most involved site for urolithiasis. Our findings are also comparable with the global trend of urolithiasis, which showed that most of the urinary calculi are localized on the upper tract (kidney) [ 49 ]. Research conducted in developing countries indicates that bladder stones are more common in certain areas, and their frequency is believed to be related to sociocultural factors and malnutrition [ 60 ]. The use of traditional herbal remedies which can delay proper medical care, and worsen stone conditions, is common in some regions of SSA [ 61 – 63 ]. Additionally, different food taboos, water scarcity, and cultural norms related to water consumption and sanitation may further contribute to the risk of bladder stones [ 64 , 65 ]. Bladder localization remained favored in older age, most likely caused by obstructions behind the bladder, which are associated with poor diuresis and urinary stasis as well as high urine concentration [ 47 ]. The pooled proportion of ureteral calculi was − 1.8% (95% CI = 0.7, 2.9),). We analyzed the combined hospital prevalence estimates of urolithiasis by gender subgroup and the result showed a high pooled prevalence in males, 6.3% (95% CI 3.1,9.6), as compared to females, 2.9% (95% CI 1.4, 4.5). The involvement of male sex hormones in the pathogenesis of urinary tract stone formation might be the possible explanation for this result [ 66 ]. This predominance can also be explained by the role of estrogen in lithogenesis, estrogen actually has a preventive effect in females by promoting the excretion of citrate in the urine, which solubilizes calcium [ 67 ]. However, the presence of comorbidities, age, and other lithogenic factors should be considered to have a conclusive report. Subgroup analysis by country showed that the highest prevalence of urolithiasis was found in Mauritian 28.1% (95%CI 24.5, 31.7) followed by Ethiopia-18.1% (1.9, 34.4), and the lowest was in Eritrea 1.0%. One possible explanation for this finding might be the difference in study participants and means of diagnosis. For example, in Mauritania, the study participants were all patients operated in the urologic ward, which may have led to an overestimation of the actual urinary tract stone prevalence. Additionally, differences in healthcare access [ 68 ], the difference in the availability of advanced imaging technology [ 54 ], and a variation in lithogenic factors including environmental and dietary habits likely contributed to these findings. Some SSA countries, like Mauritania, are located in the Saharan desert, where high temperatures and arid conditions lead to dehydration, causing concentrated urine and increasing the likelihood of stone formation [ 69 , 70 ]. Traditional diets such as leafy greens, nuts, and certain grains are common in some areas and may be high in oxalate-rich which can contribute to the formation of calcium oxalate stones [ 71 ]. Limited access to clean water in many parts of SSA leads to the consumption of untreated groundwater or hard water [ 72 ], which has been associated with an increased risk of calcium oxalate and phosphate stones [ 73 , 74 ]. In addition, low consumption of fruits and vegetables, which provide hydration and potassium to prevent stone formation [ 75 ] and diets high in animal protein and salt, which are linked to increased stone formation, are common in several SSA regions [ 76 ]. These region-specific environmental and dietary factors likely play a critical role in the variation of urolithiasis prevalence across different countries in SSA. We also assessed publication bias and a significant small study effect was observed. The trim-and-fill analysis suggested that only two studies were missing due to publication bias. After adjustment, the combined prevalence of urolithiasis SSA was slightly increased to 10.7% (95% CI: 6.3 to 15.0), suggesting the minimal impact of publication bias on the overall estimate. Although this adjustment had a minimal impact on the finding, it highlights the importance of addressing publication bias in meta-analyses. Our systematic review and metanalysis also provide a comprehensive overview of clinical patterns of urolithiasis among hospital-visiting patients using 21 studies involving 2,709 urolithiasis cases. The main clinical presentation of urolithiasis was flank pain, 58.4% (98% CL=, 45.9, 70.8). This may be attributed to a higher proportion of upper urinary tract stones than the lower tract. Flank pain, also called renal coli, results from obstruction of the renal pelvis [ 77 ], or a sustained contraction of ureteric smooth muscle as an upper urinary tract stone passes down [ 78 ]. Low back pain was the second reported clinical presentation of urolithiasis in this review, with a pooled proportion of 45.9% (98% CL=, 23.1, 68.8). It may result from stones obstructing the renal pelvis, ureter, or any kidney drainage channels. Prolonged stone blockage of the urinary tract causes stasis and backflow of urine in the urinary tubes, which can eventually cause ureter hydronephrosis and infection with sustained damage. A substantial combined clinical presentation including recurrent UTI − 16.8% (95%CI: 2.9, 30.8) and AUR/obstructive anuria- 12.2% (98% CI: 4.9, 19.0) could be the possible consequence. We also found that LUTS and nausea/or vomiting were the remarkable clinical presentation in the urinary calculi cases, with pooled estimates of 28.4 (95% CI: 17.4, 39.4) and 29.9% (95%CI: 11.1, 48.8) respectively. The pathogenic mechanisms underlying LUTS in urolithiasis are intricate and can include factors like nerve irritation, inflammation, and blockage secondary to the stone [ 79 ]. The presence of urinary calculi triggers inflammatory responses and stimulates the bladder’s nerve to become more active, which can lead to overactive bladder symptoms like frequency, urgency, and dysuria [ 79 , 80 ]. Urinary stones also bring a rise in urinary tract pressure, which may trigger the production of hormones and neurotransmitters that have an impact on the gastrointestinal system and cause vomiting/nausea [82]. Implications for public health and clinical practice The increasing prevalence of urolithiasis in SSA informs the need for targeted public health interventions focusing on the primary contributing factors. The finding emphasizes the need for early detection of urolithiasis and community awareness of risk factors and prevention strategies. Public health interventions should be implemented in specific populations, addressing preventable causes of urolithiasis. Furthermore, managing modifiable risk factors, and improving diagnostic techniques have to be implemented for the early detection of diseases that could substantially decrease the disease’s burden. The high rate of stone formation rates therefore highlights the need for healthcare professionals to enhance preventive strategies, improve diagnostic accuracy, and optimize patient care. However, this study has some limitations that need to be considered. Firstly, all the studies included in the analysis were conducted in hospitals, and most were retrospective (which are prone to bias and less informative). This could lead to an overestimation of the frequency of urolithiasis, and may not accurately represent the actual epidemiology of the problem. Secondly, only 14 countries within the SSA region were represented in the studies, which suggests that additional countries may not be effectively represented. Thirdly, we observed a significant publication bias across several subgroups, as well as significant heterogeneity between studies. These issues might influence the overall estimates of urolithiasis prevalence and clinical patterns, potentially limiting the generalizability of our results. Fourth, in most of the included studies of this analysis, the diagnosis of stone relied on routine radiography and ultrasound, which may fail to detect radiolucent stones which would result in underestimating the findings. Fifth, the a lack of detailed information regarding the specific settings in which the included studies were conducted, such as whether they were based in urology departments, emergency rooms, or any else, which may potentially contribute to the observed differences in urolithiasis prevalence. Finally, due to a shortage of free access, we were unable to conduct more database searches, including those of Scopus and EMBASE. Therefore, we suggest funding to increase database searches. Despite these limitations, our study provides valuable insights into the hospital-pooled prevalence of urolithins and its clinical patterns in the region. The evidence can serve as a foundation for making judgments and implementing preventive and early treatment policies for the condition in SSA. Conclusion This systematic review and meta-analysis provide a comprehensive prevalence and clinical presentation of urolithiasis among hospital-visiting patients in SSA. We found a pooled prevalence of 9.04%, with the kidney being the most common site of stone localization (6.2%). The clinical presentations varied across studies and countries, with flank pain, low back pain, and nausea/vomiting being the most prevalent symptoms. These findings emphasize the significance of urolithiasis as a public health issue in SSA and highlight the importance of targeted healthcare interventions and policies to address it. However, the study also identified several limitations, particularly the need for more region-specific data to better understand the actual prevalence and underlying causes of urolithiasis across SSA. Future research should focus on large-scale, community-based epidemiological studies to establish the broader scope of the problem and to assess the effectiveness of different treatment methods adapted to SSA’s unique environmental, dietary, and healthcare contexts. Addressing urolithiasis in SSA requires a multidisciplinary approach involving collaboration between policymakers, healthcare providers, and community leaders. Integrating clinical expertise with public health policy, cultural understanding, and community engagement is essential to developing effective prevention and treatment strategies. Such a collaborative effort will be key to reducing the burden of urolithiasis and improving patient outcomes across the region. documents.title: Effects of digital health interventions on muscle mass, muscle strength, and physical function in older adults with sarcopenia: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
documents.abstract:
BACKGROUND AND AIMS: Sarcopenia, an age-related progressive muscle disorder, is characterized by low muscle strength. While digital health technologies are emerging as a management tool, systematic evidence of their comprehensive effects on older adults diagnosed with sarcopenia is lacking. We therefore aimed to comprehensively evaluate the effects of digital health interventions (DHIs) on muscle mass, muscle strength, physical function, and quality of life in this specific population.
METHODS: We systematically searched PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, and the Cochrane Library for randomized controlled trials (RCTs) published up to 13 September 2025. Eligible patients were aged ≥60 years with a formal diagnosis of sarcopenia. We conducted a meta-analysis to assess intervention effects and used the GRADE system to assess the certainty of evidence.
RESULTS: Eleven RCTs with a total of 757 patients were included. The meta-analysis revealed that DHIs significantly improved skeletal muscle mass [Standardized Mean Difference (SMD) = 0.35, 95% CI: 0.13-0.57] and grip strength (SMD = 0.28, 95% CI: 0.04-0.53). However, improvements in physical function were selective, while indicators such as sit-to-stand time improved, no significant effects were found for gait speed, walking distance, or activities of daily living (ADL). The effect on quality of life (QoL) was uncertain. The certainty of evidence was moderate for skeletal muscle mass and low for grip strength.
CONCLUSION: Digital health interventions appear effective in improving muscle mass and muscle strength in older adults with sarcopenia, though their impact on physical function is selective. Technologies that provide real-time interaction and personalized feedback, particularly those based on artificial intelligence (AI) and virtual/mixed reality (VR/MR), are promising, although current evidence is preliminary. From a public health standpoint, the scalability and accessibility of DHIs represent a valuable supplementary strategy for sarcopenia management.
SYSTEMATIC REVIEW REGISTRATION: www.crd.york.ac.uk/prospero, identifier CRD420251151435.

This study was supported by the Science and Technology Innovation Project of the General Administration of Sport of China (24KJCX031) and the Humanities and the Fundamental Research Funds for the Central Universities (No. 2025JCXKSK16). pmc-status-qastatus 0 pmc-status-live yes pmc-status-embargo no pmc-status-released yes pmc-prop-open-access yes pmc-prop-olf no pmc-prop-manuscript no pmc-prop-legally-suppressed no pmc-prop-has-pdf yes pmc-prop-has-supplement yes pmc-prop-pdf-only no pmc-prop-suppress-copyright no pmc-prop-is-real-version no pmc-prop-is-scanned-article no pmc-prop-preprint no pmc-prop-in-epmc yes pmc-license-ref CC BY section-at-acceptance Aging and Public Health 1 Introduction Sarcopenia is an age-related progressive muscle disease, with low muscle strength as the core criterion for its diagnosis, confirmed by low muscle mass or low physical function according to international consensus (e.g., EWGSOP2, AWGS) ( 1 , 2 ). Sarcopenia is closely associated with a range of adverse health outcomes, including increased fall risk, disability, prolonged hospitalization, and higher mortality ( 3 , 4 ). Falls themselves are a growing public health concern globally, particularly prevalent among older adults in long-term care facilities ( 5 ). In the older adult population, the negative impact of sarcopenia on physical function is multifaceted, and other age-related issues (such as poor posture) can exacerbate functional decline. For instance, a study on older adults demonstrated that a “sway-back” posture accompanied by chronic low back pain is associated with functional limitations, not only increasing fall risk but also significantly worsening gait parameters such as speed and stride length ( 6 ). Therefore, the core muscle strength decline in sarcopenia, combined with these composite factors, places this specific population at an extremely high risk of functional limitation and falls, highlighting the urgent need for effective interventions for this fundamental problem. Exercise combined with nutritional supplementation is the current evidence-based strategy for sarcopenia management ( 7 , 8 ). However, traditional face-to-face intervention models are often challenged in practice by factors such as uneven distribution of medical resources, transportation difficulties, patient mobility limitations, and financial burdens, leading to poor long-term adherence ( 9 ). Research indicates that among individuals over 75, only 9% of men and 4% of women meet the guidelines for muscle-strengthening activities ( 10 ). The COVID-19 pandemic further underscored the urgent need to develop remote health services ( 11 ). Against this backdrop, Digital Health Interventions (DHIs) have emerged. In this study, DHIs are defined as interventions that utilize information and communication technologies—such as mobile applications, wearable devices, telehealth platforms, virtual reality (VR), or exergames to support or directly provide health-related services ( 12 , 13 ). They offer innovative solutions to overcome the barriers of traditional interventions. Previous evidence has shown that DHIs have the potential to improve muscle strength, functional capacity, and quality of life in the general older population ( 14 , 15 ), and that remote home-based exercise conducted via video conferencing can be comparable to traditional face-to-face training in improving body composition and lower limb strength ( 16 ). However, despite the increasing application of DHIs in sarcopenia management, significant research gaps persist. As noted in existing systematic reviews, current digital interventions (like mHealth) primarily focus on improving physical activity (PA) and body composition (BMI), while interventions targeting muscle function and strength remain a notable gap ( 17 , 18 ). Previous studies often included mixed populations (e.g., healthy older adults or pre-frail individuals), lacking a comprehensive assessment specifically for the high-risk group of diagnosed sarcopenia. Furthermore, many studies focused only on single outcomes (e.g., muscle strength) and failed to systematically evaluate the overall impact of DHIs on the core components of sarcopenia (muscle mass, muscle strength, multidimensional physical function) and quality of life. Finally, the application of emerging technologies such as artificial intelligence (AI) and virtual/mixed reality (VR/MR) in sarcopenia intervention is increasing, but their effectiveness lacks systematic, high-quality evidence. Therefore, this systematic review and meta-analysis aim to comprehensively evaluate the combined effects of various digital health interventions on muscle mass, muscle strength, physical function, and quality of life in older patients with diagnosed sarcopenia. This study seeks to fill the aforementioned research gaps and provide more precise evidence-based support for clinical practice. 2 Materials and methods This study’s protocol was registered with PROSPERO (Registration No.: CRD420251151435), specifying the main objectives, inclusion and exclusion criteria, interventions, control measures, and the primary and secondary outcomes planned for assessment. The implementation of this systematic review strictly adhered to the pre-registered protocol without major deviations. It was conducted and reported in strict accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA 2020) checklist ( 19 ). 2.1 Search strategy This study systematically searched PubMed, Embase, CINAHL, Web of Science, Scopus, Cochrane Library, ClinicalTrials.gov , China National Knowledge Infrastructure (CNKI), Wanfang Database, and VIP Database from their inception to 13 September 2025. The search employed a strategy combining subject headings (e.g., MeSH Terms) and free-text words, structured around four core concepts: (1) Sarcopenia (e.g., “sarcopenia,” “muscle wasting,” “muscle atrophy”); (2) Older adults (e.g., “Aged,” “older adult”); (3) Digital health interventions (e.g., “telemedicine,” “mobile app,” “Virtual Reality,” “Wearable”); and (4) Randomized controlled trials (e.g., “randomized controlled trial”). Search strategies were adapted according to the rules of each database. The complete search strings for all databases have been moved to the appendix (see Supplementary material 1 ). Additionally, we manually searched the reference lists of included articles to identify any omissions. 2.2 Inclusion and exclusion criteria Two reviewers independently screened the titles and abstracts of the literature, followed by a full-text review of potentially eligible articles to determine final inclusion. Any disagreements were resolved through discussion or third-party arbitration. Inclusion criteria were set based on the PICO-S framework: (1) Population (P): Patients aged ≥60 years and diagnosed with sarcopenia according to internationally recognized criteria (e.g., AWGS, EWGSOP2). (2) Intervention (I): Any form of digital health technology intervention. (3) Comparison (C): Usual care, health education, traditional face-to-face intervention, or no intervention. (4) Outcomes (O): At least one of the following reported: muscle mass, muscle strength, physical function, quality of life, or activities of daily living. (5) Study design (S): Randomized controlled trial (RCT). Exclusion criteria included: duplicate publications; non-original research such as conference abstracts or editorials; studies where digital technology was used only for assessment or monitoring and not as a core intervention; studies where participants had other neuromuscular diseases that could seriously affect outcome judgment; and studies with missing or unextractable key outcome data. Furthermore, articles for which the full text was unavailable were excluded, as a comprehensive quality assessment and data extraction could not be performed. This study’s search strategy focused primarily on published peer-reviewed literature and major clinical trial registries. We did not systematically search gray literature or preprint servers. The literature search was mainly limited to English and Chinese articles. To assess potential language bias, we also searched databases in other major languages (e.g., German, French, and Japanese) but found no additional RCTs that met the inclusion criteria. Therefore, the final analysis was limited to Chinese and English literature. 2.3 Data collection Two researchers independently conducted literature screening and data extraction, starting with an initial screening of titles and abstracts, followed by obtaining full texts for a second screening to finalize inclusion. Any discrepancies were resolved by discussion or consultation with a third party. A pre-designed data extraction form was used to extract the following information: (1) Basic information: first author, year of publication; (2) Population characteristics: sample size, age, sarcopenia diagnostic criteria; (3) Intervention characteristics: type of digital health technology, specific intervention content (including exercise type, prescription, frequency, duration, progression principles), supervision and feedback methods, and control group measures; (4) Outcome indicators: mean and standard deviation of skeletal muscle mass, skeletal muscle index, grip strength, walk tests, sit-to-stand tests, timed up-and-go tests, quality of life scores, and activities of daily living scores at various measurement points. For studies with incomplete data, attempts were made to contact the original authors; if unavailable, data were converted or estimated using methods recommended by the Cochrane Handbook. 2.4 Risk of bias and certainty of evidence The Cochrane Collaboration’s recommended Risk of Bias tool 2.0 (RoB 2) was used to assess the quality of included RCTs ( 20 ). The assessment covered five domains: bias arising from the randomization process, bias due to deviations from intended interventions, bias due to missing outcome data, bias in measurement of the outcome, and bias in selection of the reported result. Each domain was judged as “low risk,” “some concerns,” or “high risk,” leading to an overall risk of bias judgment for each study. The GRADE system was used to evaluate the certainty of evidence ( 21 , 22 ), assessing downgrades across five areas: risk of bias, inconsistency, indirectness, imprecision, and publication bias. The evidence quality was classified into four levels: High, Moderate, Low, or Very Low. Two reviewers independently completed the quality assessment; disagreements were resolved through discussion, with third-party expert consultation if necessary. 2.5 Data analysis RevMan 5.4 software was used for the meta-analysis. Continuous variables were analyzed using the Standardized Mean Difference (SMD) and its 95% Confidence Interval (CI) as the effect size. For physical function indicators measured in time units (e.g., TUGT, sit-to-stand time), a negative SMD value indicates improvement (time reduction). For studies reporting data at multiple time points or multiple subgroups, the data were merged using the following formulas: Combined Mean = ( n ₁ × mean₁ + n ₂ × mean₂)/( n ₁ + n ₂); Combined SD = √[(( n ₁-1) × SD₁ 2 + ( n ₂-1) × SD₂ 2 )/( n ₁ + n ₂-2)]. The χ 2 test and I 2 statistic were used to assess heterogeneity. If p > 0.10 and I 2 ≤ 50%, heterogeneity was considered acceptable, and a fixed-effect model was used. If p ≤ 0.10 or I 2 > 50%, significant heterogeneity was present, and a random-effects model was used ( 23 ). To explore potential sources of heterogeneity for results with I 2 > 50%, we pre-designed subgroup analyses based on intervention duration and technology interactivity ( 24 , 25 ). Sensitivity analysis, by sequentially removing individual studies, was used to identify sources of heterogeneity. After removing the source of heterogeneity, the I 2 value for most indicators dropped to 0% or within an acceptable range, indicating the results were robust. In this review, the number of studies included in the meta-analysis for each outcome was less than 10, and therefore, funnel plots were not used to assess publication bias ( 26 ). 3 Results 3.1 Study selection The initial search yielded 1,053 articles, including 48 from PubMed, 81 from Web of Science, 94 from Scopus, 65 from Embase, 93 from Cochrane Library, 3 from CINAHL, 214 from ClinicalTrials.gov , 112 from CNKI, 310 from Wanfang, and 33 from VIP. An additional 13 articles were supplemented through citation tracking. After removing 182 duplicates using EndNote software, 871 articles remained for title and abstract screening. A total of 812 articles that clearly did not meet the inclusion criteria were excluded. The full texts of the remaining 59 articles were obtained for detailed assessment. In the full-text assessment stage, 48 articles were excluded for the following reasons: 12 for non-compliant study design (non-RCT), 19 for non-compliant study population (not sarcopenia patients or age criteria not met), 8 for non-compliant intervention measures (not digital health intervention or used only for assessment), and 9 for other reasons (incomplete data, unextractable) (see Supplementary Table 1 ). Ultimately, 11 randomized controlled trials were included for systematic review and meta-analysis. The literature screening flow diagram is shown in Figure 1 . Among them, five were published in 2025 ( 30 , 31 , 34 , 36 , 37 ), three in 2024 ( 27 , 33 , 35 ), and one each in 2023 ( 28 ), 2022 ( 29 ), and 2017 ( 32 ). The total sample size was 757, with individual study sample sizes ranging from 23 to 142 ( 28 , 32 ). All participants were older adults aged 60 and over diagnosed with sarcopenia, with mean ages ranging from 69 to 82 years ( 31 , 32 ). Regarding diagnostic criteria, most included studies used internationally recognized standards. Specifically, most studies (nine studies) used the revised 2019 criteria from the Asian Working Group for Sarcopenia (AWGS), one study used the second version of the European Working Group on Sarcopenia in Older People (EWGSOP2) criteria ( 29 ), and another, although not explicitly citing a specific standard ( 32 ), based its diagnosis on reduced muscle mass and function, ensuring homogeneity among the study populations. In terms of study design, 8 were two-group parallel-controlled trials, and 3 were three-group parallel-controlled trials ( 27 , 30 , 37 ). The digital health interventions employed in the experimental groups showed significant diversity, with varying protocols. Some studies used smartphone apps as the intervention medium; for example, Wang et al. ( 29 ) provided a 12-week comprehensive training program of moderate-to-high intensity (2 sessions/week, 70–90 min/session) via an app that relied on automated feedback and reminders. In contrast, Zhang et al. ( 36 ) focused on a 4-week resistance training program (three sessions/week) guided by in-app videos. Other studies utilized wearable devices to promote and monitor walking activities, such as Ho et al. ( 32 ), who implemented an 8-week walking intervention with progressively increasing step goals to ensure progression, and Wu et al. ( 34 ) who conducted a 12-week structured walking program at a moderate intensity of 100 steps/min, with real-time device reminders. Some studies employed technologies offering greater real-time interactivity or artificial intelligence (AI)-driven features. Hong et al. ( 30 ) utilized Skype video conferencing to deliver real-time, one-on-one remote-supervised resistance training (three sessions/week for 12 weeks), implementing progression through gradual load increases ( 32 ). He et al. ( 27 ) and Wei et al. ( 37 ) integrated AI technology into 12-week low-intensity aerobic exercises (Tai Chi and Yi Jin Jing, respectively), using real-time text prompts or 3D human pose estimation for movement correction, and established a phased learning process. Additionally, An et al. ( 30 ) used mixed reality (MR) technology for a 4-week cognitive-motor dual-task training, with a system that automatically adjusted difficulty based on participant performance. Exergames and health management platforms were also utilized. Tuan et al. ( 35 ) used the Nintendo Switch exergame system for a 12-week multi-component training program, where the game system automatically adjusted progression and provided gamified feedback. Chitjamnogchai et al. ( 31 ) implemented a 12-week comprehensive training program using home-based virtual reality (VR) combined with real-time heart rate monitoring. Yin et al. ( 28 ) relied on a hospital-developed internet platform, combining online and offline guidance for intervention. All studies measured multiple sarcopenia-related outcomes, including muscle mass (e.g., SMM, SMI, ASMI), muscle strength (grip strength), and physical function (e.g., walking speed, sit-to-stand tests, TUGT). The overall adherence to the interventions was good, with completion rates ranging from 81.72 to 100%, and five studies achieving a 100% completion rate. 3.3 Risk of bias According to the Cochrane RoB 2.0 tool assessment, the overall quality of the 11 included studies was generally good, as shown in Figures 2 , 3 . Regarding the randomization process (D1), two studies had risks, mainly due to failure to ensure allocation sequence concealment: An et al. ( 30 ) explicitly used a “simple coin toss method”; Ho et al. ( 33 ) used “cluster randomization” and allocated by “drawing lots,” which also lacked measures to prevent allocation prediction. For deviations from intended interventions (D2), due to the nature of the interventions (e.g., remote APP vs. face-to-face or usual control), eight studies could not objectively blind participants and intervention providers ( 28 , 29 , 31 , 32 , 34–37 ), and were thus rated as “Some concerns.” Missing outcome data (D3) was the primary source of bias in this assessment. Three studies were objectively rated as “High risk” in this domain: Wang et al. ( 29 ) clearly reported a high attrition rate of 19.4% in the exercise group; Wei et al. ( 37 ) reported an attrition rate of 22.6%; and Zhang et al. ( 36 ) reported a significant differential attrition rate of 17.2% vs. 6.9%. According to Cochrane standards, because these three studies did not report (not reported) using intention-to-treat (ITT) analysis to handle these high and unbalanced missing data, their bias risk was rated as high. Additionally, one study ( 28 ) was rated “Some concerns” for not reporting any attrition data at the 6-month follow-up. For bias in measurement of the outcome (D4), five studies were rated “Some concerns” for not reporting whether outcome assessors were blinded ( 28 , 29 , 31 , 33 , 37 ). For bias in the selection of the reported result (D5), eight studies were rated Low risk ( 27–29 , 31 , 33 , 35–37 ). Three studies had “Some concerns” ( 30 , 32 , 34 ), for objective reasons, including not reporting trial registration or explicitly stating retrospective registration. Overall, three studies were rated “Overall High risk” due to objective flaws in D3 ( 29 , 36 , 37 ). Six studies were rated “Some concerns” ( 28 , 30–34 ). Two studies were rated “Low risk” ( 27 , 35 ). This result suggests that the findings of this meta-analysis must be interpreted with close attention to potential bias from missing data. The pooled analysis for skeletal muscle mass showed a statistically significant improvement (five studies, n = 328; SMD = 0.35, 95% CI: 0.13–0.57, p < 0.01), with high consistency among studies ( I 2 = 0%) (see Figure 4 ). Similarly, a significant positive effect was observed for skeletal muscle mass index (nine studies, n = 576; SMD = 0.26, 95% CI: 0.02–0.51, p = 0.04) (see Figure 5 ). To explore the moderate heterogeneity ( I 2 = 52%) in skeletal muscle mass index, we conducted a sensitivity analysis. The results indicated that Wu et al. ( 34 ) was the primary source of heterogeneity; after its removal, heterogeneity was eliminated ( I 2 = 0%), and the pooled effect size remained statistically significant (SMD = 0.18, p = 0.04), confirming the robustness of the result. Furthermore, the pre-specified subgroup analyses ( Supplementary Figures 1 , 2 ) showed no statistically significant differences in effects between groups, whether grouped by intervention duration (>8 weeks vs. ≤ 8 weeks) or technology interactivity (high vs. low) ( p > 0.05). The meta-analysis for grip strength, a core diagnostic criterion for sarcopenia, confirmed this improvement (nine studies, n = 576; SMD = 0.28, 95% CI: 0.04–0.53, p = 0.02) (see Figure 6 ). This analysis had moderate heterogeneity ( I 2 = 52%). Sensitivity analysis indicated that Yin et al. ( 28 ) was the main source of heterogeneity; its removal eliminated heterogeneity ( I 2 = 0%), and the result remained statistically significant (SMD = 0.20, p = 0.04), demonstrating robustness. Subsequent subgroup analyses ( Supplementary Figures 3 , 4 ) showed that neither intervention duration nor technology interactivity significantly explained the heterogeneity (between-group p > 0.05). Specifically, observed improvements included a significant reduction in the time for a fixed-number sit-to-stand test (two studies; SMD = −0.63, p = 0.02) ( Supplementary Figure 5 ), suggesting a potential benefit for lower limb power. However, the result for the Timed Up and Go Test (TUGT) (six studies; SMD = 0.32, p = 0.05) ( Supplementary Figure 6 ) was at the statistical threshold, showing no significant difference. This improvement did not extend to all physical function indicators. Notably, no statistically significant changes were observed in key mobility metrics, including gait speed over a specified distance (six studies; p = 0.73) ( Supplementary Figure 7 ) and walking distance in a specified time (two studies; p = 0.40) ( Supplementary Figure 8 ). Furthermore, the number of sit-to-stands in a specified time (two studies; p = 0.12) ( Supplementary Figure 9 ) also showed no significant improvement. 3.4.4 Secondary outcomes Assessment of secondary outcomes also revealed uncertainty. For Quality of Life (QoL), the pooled analysis initially showed a moderate improvement (five studies; SMD = 0.47, p = 0.02) ( Supplementary Figure 10 ). However, this result had moderate heterogeneity ( I 2 = 57%) and lacked robustness. Sensitivity analysis showed that after excluding He et al. ( 27 ), the pooled effect lost statistical significance (SMD = 0.31, p = 0.34), suggesting the current evidence is inconclusive. Meanwhile, for Activities of Daily Living (ADL), the pooled analysis showed no significant difference compared to the control group (three studies; SMD = 0.43, p = 0.39), and this result was affected by very high heterogeneity ( I 2 = 91%) ( Supplementary Figure 11 ). The certainty of evidence for skeletal muscle mass was moderate (five studies, 328 patients) ( 29 , 32 , 34–36 ). This outcome was downgraded due to the inclusion of high-risk-of-bias studies. The evidence for two core indicators, skeletal muscle mass index ( 27 , 28 , 33 , 35–37 ) and grip strength ( 27 , 28 , 33–37 ), was low (nine studies each, 576 patients). Both were downgraded twice: once for high risk of bias and once for moderate heterogeneity. The evidence for physical function indicators was mostly low or very low. Gait speed (six studies, 253 patients) ( 27 , 34–36 ), TUGT (six studies, 267 patients) ( 27 , 32 , 36 , 37 ), and the number of sit-to-stand in prescribed time ( 29 , 36 ) were all rated as “low” certainty, downgraded for high risk of bias and imprecision. Time of sit-to-stand in prescribed number (two studies, 128 patients) ( 27 , 28 ) was rated “moderate,” downgraded only for the small number of studies. The evidence for walking distance (two studies, 104 patients) ( 31 , 36 ) was “very low,” receiving triple downgrades for high risk of bias, high heterogeneity, and serious imprecision. Quality of Life (five studies, 224 patients) ( 27 , 30 , 37 ) was rated “low.” Activities of Daily Living (three studies, 225 patients) ( 28 , 30 , 36 ) was also rated “very low” due to high risk of bias, serious heterogeneity, and imprecision. Notably, as the number of studies for each outcome was less than 10, publication bias could not be assessed via funnel plots, which may affect the overall confidence in the evidence. Given that the evidence for most primary outcomes was rated “moderate” to “very low,” the conclusions of this study regarding the effectiveness of DHIs should be interpreted with caution.
