Based on data from 11 RCTs involving 757 patients, our main findings show that DHIs are significantly effective in improving the core indicators of sarcopenia. This was particularly evident for muscle mass, where skeletal muscle mass (five studies, SMD = 0.35, 95% CI: 0.13–0.57) showed a statistically significant improvement with high consistency ( I 2 = 0%), and the evidence was rated as moderate certainty. Similarly, grip strength, the core diagnostic criterion for sarcopenia, also showed a significant increase (nine studies, SMD = 0.28, 95% CI: 0.04–0.53), with moderate heterogeneity ( I 2 = 52%) and low certainty evidence. Although the observed effect sizes (SMD 0.28–0.35) are in the small-to-moderate range, their significance is important in the specific clinical context of sarcopenia. First, sarcopenia is an age-related progressive muscle disease, placing patients on a trajectory of continuous functional decline and at high risk for adverse outcomes (e.g., falls, disability). In this context, any statistically significant positive change, even if modest, may represent a containment of this decline, which is crucial for preventing disability. However, the intervention’s impact on physical function was selective; while sit-to-stand time significantly improved (two studies, SMD = –0.63, p = 0.02), no significant improvements were seen in mobility indicators such as gait speed and walking distance. Overall, the clinical implication of these findings is that they provide strong evidence-based support for integrating DHIs as a feasible and effective strategy into the comprehensive management of sarcopenia, especially for patient groups with limited access to traditional rehabilitation services. 4.2 Comparison with other studies and mechanistic analysis Our findings are both consistent with and distinct from previous research. In the DHI field, an umbrella review by Longhini et al. ( 38 ) focused on the impact of wearables on physical activity. It found that while wearables effectively improved PA in middle-aged adults, the results in older adult subgroups were inconsistent and uncertain. This finding aligns closely with our observation that functional mobility (i.e., walking ability) did not significantly improve, highlighting that translating the benefits of digital interventions into functional mobility improvements in sarcopenic patients remains challenging and selective. Compared to the systematic review by Makizako et al. ( 14 ), which focused on healthy older adults, our study’s focus on diagnosed sarcopenia patients reveals slightly lower but more clinically specific effect sizes, possibly reflecting the reality that sarcopenic patients have lower functional baselines and greater difficulty improving. Notably, these interventions can be categorized by technology integration and delivery mode into asynchronous and synchronous models. Most studies used asynchronous models, providing preset content via mobile apps or VR systems and relying on automated feedback or data monitoring; this model is flexible and scalable ( 34 , 37 ). A few studies used synchronous models, such as real-time one-on-one remote supervised training via video conferencing ( 32 ), which provides stronger personalized guidance and social support. These differences in delivery mode, along with the intervention content itself, constitute the complex mechanisms by which DHIs function. It must be emphasized that this study did not directly assess the physiological or psychological mechanisms of the interventions. Therefore, the following discussion is based primarily on indirect evidence and theoretical inference from prior literature, intended to provide a possible explanatory framework for our observed results rather than empirical conclusions ( 39 ). Based on this premise, the potential mechanisms of DHIs may involve multiple levels. First, from a neuromuscular adaptation perspective, resistance training reportedly improves motor unit recruitment and neuromuscular coordination ( 40 ). Visual feedback and real-time guidance in DHIs might enhance motor cortex activation and motor learning efficiency ( 30 ), while VR may promote neuroplasticity through enhanced sensorimotor integration ( 41 ). Second, behavioral change mechanisms likely played a significant role. Instant feedback, goal setting, and gamification elements in DHIs may help enhance patient self-efficacy and intrinsic motivation, thereby improving long-term adherence ( 42 , 43 ). From a molecular level, regular exercise is known to regulate the mTOR signaling pathway related to muscle protein synthesis and reduce inflammatory factors, although this review did not measure these biomarkers ( 44 ). Furthermore, cognitive engagement may be a unique advantage of DHIs. Many interventions (e.g., MR training) require cognitive-motor dual-task processing; this type of training is believed to improve executive function ( 45 ). However, our results showed that improvements in physical function were selective, suggesting that the specific method of cognitive engagement and the use of cognitive strategies are critical. First, real-world gait in older adults is rarely a single task but rather a dual task. A study on older adults confirmed that cognitive strategies induced by positive expectancy (i.e., placebo effect) significantly reduced dual-task costs and improved gait performance ( 46 ). This suggests that the positive expectancy built by DHIs may be a key factor in enhancing functional outcomes. Second, the effectiveness of cognitive strategy is modulated by attentional focus. Research has shown that the enhancing effect of cognitive intervention on muscle strength only occurs when participants adopt an internal focus of attention; performance was inhibited with an external focus ( 47 ). This finding has direct implications for the different DHI types assessed in our review. Therefore, the cognitive design of a DHI may be a key moderating variable, perhaps explaining the selective functional improvements observed in our study. Sociopsychological factors also cannot be ignored; remote supervision and virtual socialization may reduce feelings of social isolation, and social support is linked to sarcopenia improvement ( 48 , 49 ). Finally, these mechanistic speculations, based mainly on indirect evidence and theory ( 50 ), help explain why the effects of DHIs can be comparable to some traditional face-to-face interventions, but they still require future research with corresponding biomarkers and psychometrics for direct validation. 4.3 Study limitations The innovation of this study lies in its first systematic inclusion of evidence on the application of emerging technologies such as artificial intelligence and mixed reality in sarcopenia intervention, and ensuring the homogeneity of the study population based on international diagnostic standards, providing a reference for the effectiveness of digital health interventions. Although this systematic review provides important evidence on the effects of digital health interventions on older adults with sarcopenia, several limitations exist that require cautious interpretation of the results. First, at the study level, the number of included RCTs is relatively limited, the number of studies for some outcome measures (such as walking distance, sit-to-stand test) is insufficient, and some studies have small sample sizes. This limits the statistical power and generalizability of the results. The small sample sizes in some studies may lead to imprecise effect estimates, as reflected in the wide confidence intervals for several outcome measures. The heterogeneity of interventions is another important limitation; the included studies covered various technological forms, from mobile apps and wearable devices to virtual reality and artificial intelligence, with intervention durations ranging from 4 to 12 weeks. While this heterogeneity reflects the diversity of digital health technologies, it also increases the difficulty of determining the optimal intervention protocol. Furthermore, more than half of the studies had concerns regarding the risk of bias from missing outcome data, which might overestimate the true effect of the interventions. At the research level, issues such as non-uniformity of measurement methods, the inability to assess publication bias using funnel plots, and the fact that studies were mainly from Asian countries, which may limit the generalizability of the results, still exist. In particular, as mentioned in the methods section, this study’s search strategy did not cover gray literature or preprint servers, and coupled with the fact that the number of studies included for each outcome was less than 10, it was impossible to effectively assess publication bias using funnel plots. Therefore, this study may have failed to include some unpublished negative result studies, posing a potential risk of overestimating the true intervention effects. More importantly, this study failed to deeply explore the adherence to and real-world usability of the interventions. Although the included studies reported generally high completion rates, this does not fully represent high adherence to these technologies in real-world, non-clinically supervised environments. In actual implementation, long-term use by older adults is constrained by various complex factors, none of which were fully evaluated in the current studies. Among these, accessibility and digital literacy constitute the primary barriers, as the digital divide may exclude some older adults lacking equipment or skills from the outset. The inadequacy of age-friendly design in devices is another common problem; many technologies are designed with younger users as the target, and their complex interfaces and operational logic undoubtedly create difficulties for older users. Moreover, psychosocial factors should not be ignored, such as the potential resistance of some older adults to using technologies perceived as “assistive” or “monitoring” due to “stigma.” In addition, this study lacks an assessment of the mechanisms of intervention action. None of the included studies reported physiological mechanism parameters such as inflammatory markers or muscle protein synthesis indicators, nor did they assess psychological mediators like self-efficacy or exercise motivation, limiting the understanding of the intrinsic mechanisms by which digital health technologies improve sarcopenia. 4.4 Practical implications Although the evidence from this study is still preliminary, its results can nonetheless offer some guidance for clinical practice. For the specific population focused on older adults with diagnosed sarcopenia, digital health interventions can be considered as a potential supplementary management strategy, based on the high-to-moderate quality evidence showing improvements in muscle mass and muscle strength. This is particularly applicable to patients who have difficulty accessing traditional rehabilitation due to geographical location, mobility issues, or financial burdens. When developing individualized treatment plans, clinicians should prioritize intervention models that have been proven effective, such as comprehensive programs including resistance and balance training ( 51 , 52 ). They should also strengthen gait training and dynamic balance exercises, based on this study’s findings regarding the selective nature of improvements in physical function. For technology selection, choices can be flexible based on the patient’s digital literacy and preferences. A hybrid model could be adopted, providing necessary face-to-face guidance during the initial phase of the intervention to ensure safety and accuracy. From a policy and research perspective, the results of this study support the integration of digital health technologies into the prevention and management systems for sarcopenia in older adults. Policymakers should consider establishing standardized guidelines and quality certification, including effective interventions in health insurance coverage, investing in digital infrastructure, and conducting skills training for healthcare professionals. At the same time, future research should focus on addressing existing evidence gaps, including conducting large-sample, multicenter RCTs covering other populations, performing head-to-head comparison studies of different technologies, evaluating long-term effects, and exploring the potential of artificial intelligence in developing personalized protocols. Furthermore, it is necessary to establish the minimum effective dose and optimal combination model for interventions, and to elucidate their mechanisms of action by including biomarkers and psychological scales. Furthermore, research exploration should transcend existing technological frameworks, focusing on potential technologies with higher levels of integration and intelligence. First, the application of wearable devices should be deepened, expanding from step counting to collecting multi-dimensional data such as gait and balance. Second, it is crucial to use this data to develop predictive algorithms, with the aim of identifying functional decline in advance or predicting fall risk, thereby achieving active prevention. Finally, developing more complex real-time feedback systems is a direction worth exploring, for example, combining artificial intelligence coaches with augmented/virtual reality (AR/VR) technology to dynamically adjust training based on the user’s real-time physiological data, providing a highly personalized and immersive experience. The fusion of these cutting-edge technologies may help older adults with sarcopenia build a closed-loop, intelligent, and efficient management solution. 5 Conclusion This systematic review and meta-analysis, for the first time, evaluated the comprehensive effects of digital health interventions specifically targeting older adults with diagnosed sarcopenia. Based on evidence from 11 randomized controlled trials, these interventions appear to significantly improve patients’ muscle mass and muscle strength, but their effect on improving overall physical function (especially walking ability) is not yet clear, showing some selectivity. The range of digital technologies evaluated in this study was broad, covering everything from basic mobile applications and wearable monitoring devices to more interactive remote video guidance, exergames, virtual reality, and artificial intelligence real-time feedback systems. Overall, technologies capable of providing real-time, interactive, and personalized feedback show good application prospects. Although the number of studies based on emerging technologies such as artificial intelligence (AI) and virtual/mixed reality (VR/MR) was still small in this review, and the evidence remains preliminary, the real-time interaction and personalized feedback features they demonstrate suggest their potential as future management tools. Therefore, digital health interventions, especially those capable of providing personalized guidance and feedback, offer new possibilities for the future of personalized and remote sarcopenia management. From a public health perspective, the findings of this study are positive; considering the inherent scalability and accessibility of digital interventions, they provide a promising supplementary strategy for addressing the increasingly severe challenges of sarcopenia management in the context of global aging. documents.title: The Burden of Informal Caregiving for Adults with Musculoskeletal Conditions: A Systematic Review.
documents.abstract:
BACKGROUND AND OBJECTIVE: Informal caregivers play a critical role in supporting individuals with musculoskeletal conditions. This systematic review aimed to evaluate the psychological and economic burdens associated with caregiving for musculoskeletal conditions.
METHODS: We conducted a systematic review in accordance with PRISMA (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic reviews and Meta-Analyses) guidelines, searching MEDLINE, Embase, CINAHL, EconLIT, and APA PsycINFO for studies published between 2000 and April 2025. Studies were eligible if they examined the psychological and economic burden of informal caregiving for adults with musculoskeletal conditions. Screening and data extraction were conducted using EndNote 21 and Covidence. Risk of bias was assessed using the CASP checklist for psychological burden studies and the EVERS criteria for economic burden studies. Data were synthesized narratively. An exploratory meta-analysis of informal care hours was conducted using a subset of studies with sufficient statistical data.
RESULTS: A total of 41 studies were included, with 24 reporting psychological burdens, 16 economic burdens, and one for both. Caregiving burden included emotional, social, financial, and time-related impacts, impacting the caregivers' quality of life. Higher anxiety and depression were correlated with a greater caregiver burden. Informal care costs varied by musculoskeletal condition type, location, severity, intensity, and valuation method. Reported informal care hours showed substantial variation across studies. The overall risk of bias across included studies was low.
CONCLUSIONS: This systematic review highlights the considerable psychological, economic, and time-related burdens faced by informal caregivers of individuals with musculoskeletal conditions. Caregivers face high stress, physical strain, and opportunity costs. The lack of standardized assessments hinders accurate burden quantification, economic evaluation, and policy responses. Future efforts should focus on adopting consistent measurement instruments and valuation methods, alongside implementing structured policies, financial support, and psychological interventions to better support the caregivers.

Abstract Background and Objective Informal caregivers play a critical role in supporting individuals with musculoskeletal conditions. This systematic review aimed to evaluate the psychological and economic burdens associated with caregiving for musculoskeletal conditions. Methods We conducted a systematic review in accordance with PRISMA (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic reviews and Meta-Analyses) guidelines, searching MEDLINE, Embase, CINAHL, EconLIT, and APA PsycINFO for studies published between 2000 and April 2025. Studies were eligible if they examined the psychological and economic burden of informal caregiving for adults with musculoskeletal conditions. Screening and data extraction were conducted using EndNote 21 and Covidence. Risk of bias was assessed using the CASP checklist for psychological burden studies and the EVERS criteria for economic burden studies. Data were synthesized narratively. An exploratory meta-analysis of informal care hours was conducted using a subset of studies with sufficient statistical data. Results A total of 41 studies were included, with 24 reporting psychological burdens, 16 economic burdens, and one for both. Caregiving burden included emotional, social, financial, and time-related impacts, impacting the caregivers’ quality of life. Higher anxiety and depression were correlated with a greater caregiver burden. Informal care costs varied by musculoskeletal condition type, location, severity, intensity, and valuation method. Reported informal care hours showed substantial variation across studies. The overall risk of bias across included studies was low. Conclusions This systematic review highlights the considerable psychological, economic, and time-related burdens faced by informal caregivers of individuals with musculoskeletal conditions. Caregivers face high stress, physical strain, and opportunity costs. The lack of standardized assessments hinders accurate burden quantification, economic evaluation, and policy responses. Future efforts should focus on adopting consistent measurement instruments and valuation methods, alongside implementing structured policies, financial support, and psychological interventions to better support the caregivers. Key Points for Decision Makers Informal caregiving (unpaid caregiving) is a significant but under-quantified contributor to the burden of chronic illness, particularly in musculoskeletal conditions, which are a leading cause of global disability. This systematic review synthesizes global evidence on the psychological, economic, and time-related burdens faced by informal caregivers of people with musculoskeletal conditions. Findings underscore the need for policy reforms and standardized methods for measuring and valuation to recognize and support informal caregivers in musculoskeletal care planning. Introduction Musculoskeletal conditions (MSCs) are highly prevalent and represent the leading cause of disability worldwide, according to estimates from the Global Burden of Disease Study 2019 [ 1 ]. There are over 150 MSCs affecting joints (osteoarthritis, rheumatoid arthritis, psoriatic arthritis, spondylarthritis), bones (osteoporosis, osteopenia, fractures), and muscles (sarcopenia). Musculoskeletal conditions also include inflammatory diseases such as connective tissue disorders and vasculitis, and pain-related conditions (back, neck, fibromyalgia) [ 2 ]. Affecting 1.71 billion individuals globally, MSCs impose a substantial health burden [ 1 ]. Persons with a musculoskeletal condition (PwMSC) have an increased risk of developing additional chronic diseases and mental health problems [ 3 , 4 ]. Musculoskeletal conditions are also the most significant contributor to years lived with disability, with approximately 149 million years lived with disability, accounting for 17% of all years lived with disability worldwide [ 1 ]. Informal care refers to unpaid assistance provided by family, friends, or neighbors [ 5 ]. Informal caregivers are typically individuals offering ongoing unpaid support with Activities of Daily Living (ADLs) for someone with a chronic illness or disability [ 6 ]. Activities of Daily Living are categorized as basic or instrumental). Basic ADLs include self-care tasks such as hygiene, dressing, toileting, mobility, and eating, while instrumental ADLs involve more complex activities like managing finances, taking medications, meal preparation, housekeeping, and laundry [ 7 ]. Caregiver burden refers to the emotional and physical strain caregivers face when caring for patients with chronic illnesses, often enhanced by their multiple responsibilities [ 8 , 9 ]. Studies show that informal caregivers tend to have poorer physical, mental, and social health compared with non-carers [ 8 , 10 – 12 ]. While caregiving can also bring positive outcomes, like affection, empathy, and community support [ 13 – 17 ], it may lead to significant stress, particularly when it is intensive [ 18 ]. Informal caregiving also has economic consequences, affecting labor participation and incurring costs like time, out-of-pocket expenses, and employment impacts [ 19 – 21 ], all of which can impact caregivers’ quality of life (QoL) [ 22 – 25 ]. The type of condition can significantly influence the nature and intensity of informal caregiving demands [ 26 ]. Persons with a MSC often experience distinct manifestations such as chronic pain and functional limitations [ 27 ], needing support with daily activities to maintain independence [ 22 , 28 ]. Caregivers of individuals with MSCs often face substantial physical demands, such as providing mobility assistance and managing pain — tasks that differ markedly from the cognitive and behavioral supervision typically required in caregiving for conditions like dementia [ 27 – 34 ]. For instance, studies have reported that caregivers of individuals with rheumatoid arthritis experience significant physical strain and considerable disruption to their daily routines [ 32 , 35 ]. One study using consistent valuation methods found that caregivers of individuals with rheumatoid arthritis spent approximately 7 more hours per week on household tasks than those caring for stroke survivors, although no formal statistical comparison was reported [ 36 ]. Furthermore, MSCs, peaking between the age of 50–54 years, worsen with age [ 1 ], leading to complications like fractures and falls, thereby increasing the caregiver burden [ 37 ]. Studies show caregivers of people with chronic conditions, including MSCs, often experience MSCs and back pain themselves [ 38 – 41 ].While caregiving burdens have been studied, they are rarely disease specific [ 42 – 47 ]. Research has primarily focused on dementia [ 47 – 49 ] and cancer [ 42 – 44 ], though the type of condition, caregiving duration, and patient functionality are key factors contributing to the caregiver burden [ 8 , 26 , 50 , 51 ]. To develop more tailored interventions and support, it is important to understand how different diseases impact the caregiver burden. To date, no systematic reviews have evaluated the economic and psychological burden of caring for PwMSC. Existing evidence has focused primarily on qualitative insights from caregivers’ lived experiences for chronic musculoskeletal pain [ 17 ]. This review addresses that gap by systematically assessing the broader burden of caregiving for MSCs, to inform targeted support strategies. Methods Protocol and Registration This systematic review was conducted according to a pre-specified protocol and has been registered in the PROSPERO database (ID: CRD42024566143). The review follows the guidelines outlined in the PRISMA (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic reviews and Meta-Analyses) statement [ 52 ]. Study Design and Search Strategy A systematic search was conducted across multiple databases, including MEDLINE, Embase, EconLIT, CINAHL, and APA PsycINFO. The research strategies consisted of concepts combining MSCs, informal care, and burden to identify relevant studies. For MSCs, terms such as “musculoskeletal disorders,” “arthritis,” “back pain,” “spinal disorders,” and “osteoporosis” were used. To capture informal care, terms like “informal caregiving,” “family care,” and “unpaid care” were included. To explore burden, the search included terms reflecting psychological (e.g., “caregiver stress,” “depression,” “mental health”), physical (e.g., “caregiver burnout,” “physical strain”), and economic impacts (e.g., “financial burden,” “indirect costs,” “productivity loss”). Broader terms like “disease burden” and “care burden” were used to ensure comprehensive coverage. Boolean operators and database-specific vocabulary, including MeSH terms, were applied to retrieve studies at the intersection of these key areas. The strategy was developed in collaboration with a librarian, who assisted in refining search terms and selecting appropriate databases to maximize the retrieval of high-quality studies aligned with the review objectives. The detailed search strategy, including an example from MEDLINE, is provided in Appendix 1 of the Electronic Supplementary Material (ESM). Inclusion and Exclusion Criteria We included English-language studies published after 2000 up to April 2025 that examined the burden of informal caregiving for adults with MSCs or conditions with significant musculoskeletal manifestations. For economic burden, eligible studies reported extractable informal care costs either as stand-alone estimates or combined with indirect or direct non-medical costs. Studies were excluded if they relied on informal care data from primary research already included in this review or used modeling approaches not based on original data. Pediatric caregiving studies (under 18 years of age) were also excluded because of differing caregiver roles. Only original peer-reviewed research articles were included. Non-original publications such as reviews, editorials, commentaries, protocols, opinion pieces, case reports, and conference abstracts were excluded. In this review, psychological burden was defined as the emotional, cognitive, and mental strain experienced by caregivers, including stress, anxiety, depression, and broader effects on well-being and QoL. This includes the time-related burden, such as schedule disruption and time pressure, as measured by validated caregiver burden tools. This conceptualization builds on established frameworks [ 53 – 59 ] and includes physical manifestations of caregiver stress, such as pain, fatigue, and physical strain [ 60 ]. The search was limited to English because of time and resource constraints related to translation. Data Extraction References were managed using EndNote 21 [ 61 ] and screened in Covidence [ 62 ]. After duplicate removal in both platforms, two reviewers (NA and ND) independently screened titles and abstracts, followed by full-text reviews. Disagreements were resolved by a third reviewer (LG). Relevant data from included studies were extracted into Microsoft Excel ® by one reviewer (NA) and randomly validated by two others (ND and LG), with disagreements resolved by consensus. To enable comparison, all costs were adjusted to 2023 US dollars using PPP conversion rates from the IMF World Economic Outlook Database [ 63 ]. When studies reported costs in a foreign currency (e.g., Euros in a Swedish study), values were first converted back to the original currency using the reported exchange rate and date before inflation adjustment and PPP conversion. Risk of Bias Assessment We assessed methodological quality using the EVERS criteria for economic studies [ 64 ] and the CASP checklist for cross-sectional studies [ 65 ]. One reviewer (NA) conducted the assessments, with one third randomly validated by a second reviewer (ND); disagreements were resolved by consensus. Each item was rated as: Yes’ (criterion clearly met), No’ (criterion not met), CT’ (cannot tell, because of insufficient information), or ‘NA’ (not applicable). Studies were classified as high quality if they received a ‘Yes’ rating on at least 75% of applicable items. Full descriptions of the checklists are provided in Appendix 2 of the ESM. Exploratory Meta-Analysis (Informal Care Hours) An exploratory meta-analysis was conducted to synthesize informal care hours for MSCs using a subset of eligible studies that reported both mean and standard deviation values. A random-effects model was applied to account for heterogeneity across studies owing to differences in geographic regions and MSC type. Given the small number of studies and substantial heterogeneity, this analysis was exploratory in nature. The results are presented to illustrate potential patterns rather than to provide a generalizable average across all MSCs. Details of the analysis, including assumptions, and the forest plot, are provided in Appendix 3 of the ESM. Data analyses were conducted using Stata ® Statistical Software, Release 18 (StataCorp LLC, College Station, TX, USA). Results Study Selection The original search of studies was conducted on 10 July, 2024, followed by an updated search on 8 April, 2025 to capture newly published studies. A total of 41 studies were included for data extraction: 25 reported on psychological burden, 15 on economic burden, and one addressed both [ 66 ]. Following the PRISMA guidelines, the detailed results are displayed in Fig. 1 . Some studies examined the overall burden of MSC caregiving rather than specific conditions [ 58 , 59 , 68 , 71 ]. Most psychological burden studies used cross-sectional designs, though some employed prospective cohort approaches [ 77 , 87 , 94 ]. Economic studies were largely based on a cost-of-illness (COI) analysis ( n = 11) [ 70 , 80 , 81 , 88 – 91 , 95 – 98 ], with the majority adopting a societal perspective; one study used a payer perspective [ 97 ]. The timeframe over which informal care costs were varied across studies, with 1 year being the most common ( n = 10) [ 73 , 80 , 81 , 88 – 91 , 95 , 96 , 98 ]. Sample sizes ranged widely across the studies, from as few as 43 participants in cross-sectional surveys [ 92 ] to more than 57,000 participants in registry-based economic evaluations [ 89 ], with larger studies using registries or surveys [ 88 , 89 , 91 , 99 ]. Risk of Bias Assessment A total of 26 psychological burden studies were evaluated using the CASP framework, with the majority (over 85%) scoring high overall quality, having met at least 75% of applicable checklist items. All studies met the criteria for addressing focused research questions and using appropriate methods. However, limitations were evident across several domains. Recruitment processes were unclear in some studies [ 57 , 66 , 86 , 87 ]. Approximately one third of studies [ 32 , 35 , 76 , 79 , 85 , 92 , 93 ] lacked sufficient participants to minimize the role of chance. Furthermore, one study was rated as “No” for applicability to local populations, limiting generalizability [ 69 ] (Table 1 of the ESM). All economic burden studies met the criteria defined in the study characteristics checklist (Table 2 of the ESM). Some studies were rated lower in quality owing to the absence of subgroup data [ 70 , 82 , 97 , 99 ], which may be important for understanding the impact of MSC severity and type. Sensitivity analyses were not conducted in most studies [ 66 , 70 , 73 , 78 , 80 – 82 , 88 , 95 , 97 ] and several lacked discussion of generalizability [ 66 , 70 , 72 , 73 , 98 ], or distributional implications [ 70 , 88 , 91 , 96 , 98 , 99 ], limiting the applicability of findings to broader settings. Characteristics of Caregivers from Included Studies Caregivers were predominantly middle-aged or older, typically in their late 40s to early 60s, though some studies included younger caregivers [ 66 , 85 ]. Most psychological burden studies reported female caregivers [ 32 , 57 , 59 , 66 , 68 , 69 ], whereas three economic studies reported a male majority, with the percentage of male caregivers having a range from 68% [ 66 ] to 76% [ 72 ]. Some studies did not specify participants by sex. Most caregivers were primary caregivers, typically spouses or close family members [ 32 , 35 , 57 ]. Disease duration and caregiving time varied widely, with some studies reporting over a decade of caregiving [ 32 , 57 ], while others lacked this information [ 67 , 71 , 77 , 92 , 93 ]. In the majority of economic burden studies (11 out of 16), care recipients completed questionnaires on informal care hours and associated costs, while in five studies, caregivers themselves provided caregiver-specific information [ 66 , 72 , 73 , 78 , 81 ]. In total, studies covered care recipients with 14 types of MSCs, with the majority (nine) focusing on arthritis [ 32 , 35 , 56 , 57 , 67 , 69 , 75 , 77 , 79 ]; four studies on spinal conditions (e.g., SCIs) [ 83 – 86 ]; three studies each on osteoporotic fractures [ 66 , 87 , 100 ], muscular disorders [ 56 , 93 , 101 ], and chronic pain conditions [ 71 , 74 , 76 ]; and four studies on MSCs not classified by types [ 58 , 59 , 68 , 94 ]. Fourteen studies assessed multiple domains of psychological burden, including emotional, social, physical, and time-related aspects such as disrupted schedules and time constraints [ 57 – 59 , 66 – 69 , 71 , 76 , 79 , 92 , 93 , 100 , 101 ]. Additional domains included anxiety and/or depression (6 studies) [ 35 , 59 , 69 , 71 , 74 , 93 ], caregiver strain (three studies) [ 77 , 87 , 94 ], caregiver reaction (two studies) [ 56 , 57 ], mental health (two studies) [ 79 , 100 ], physical pain and/disability (two studies) [ 84 , 85 ], and marital satisfaction (one study) [ 74 ] (Table 1 ). Measurement Approaches and Instruments The Zarit Burden Interview (ZBI) was the most frequently used (seven studies) [ 66 , 69 , 71 , 79 , 92 , 93 , 101 ] to assess physical, emotional, social, and financial burden. The Caregiver Burden Inventory (CBI) was used in five studies [ 58 , 59 , 67 , 68 , 100 ], to assess burden across time-dependence, developmental, physical, social, and emotional domains. The Caregiver Reaction Assessment (CRA) was applied in three studies [ 32 , 56 , 57 ], to capture both positive and negative aspects of caregiving. The Caregiver Strain Index [ 77 , 87 ] and Oswestry Disability Index [ 84 , 85 ] were used in two studies to assess caregiver strain and disability, respectively. Six studies [ 35 , 59 , 69 , 71 , 74 , 93 ] employed a range of instruments to assess anxiety, depression, and emotional distress. These measures included the Centre for Epidemiology-Depression, Depression, Anxiety, and Stress Scale (DASS-21), and the Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale. The Beck Depression Inventory and Beck Anxiety Inventory assessed depression and anxiety, while the Mood and Anxiety Symptom Questionnaire measured distress, depression, and anxiety severity. Other instruments, used in single studies, assessed the caregiving burden, distress severity, hostility, perceived injustice, marital adjustment, and pain levels [ 71 , 74 , 76 , 85 ], with specific details available in Table 1 . Key Findings Caregivers reported moderate-to-high levels of burden across different scales, including the ZBI, CBI, and Caregiver Strain Index, as defined by each instrument’s scoring criteria, with time-dependence burden being the most commonly reported challenge [ 58 , 67 , 68 , 100 ]. Caregivers of rheumatoid arthritis and osteoporotic fracture patients reported particularly high burden scores [ 66 , 69 ]. Some caregiver distress decreases over time, particularly in cases where care recipients show recovery [ 77 , 87 ]. Studies using scales like Centre for Epidemiology-Depression and Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale found that caregivers of rheumatoid arthritis and patients with spinal muscular atrophy exhibited higher rates of depressive symptoms and anxiety, particularly in high-burden cases, with burden levels measured using the ZBI and compared within caregiver groups [ 69 , 93 ]. In contrast, caregivers of persons with chronic musculoskeletal pain and MSCs not classified by type exhibited relatively lower distress levels on standardized scales [ 59 , 71 ]. Psychological well-being, as measured by the Psychological General Well-Being Index, showed that caregivers’ mental health was associated with the well-being of the patients they cared for [ 100 ]. Marital satisfaction was also assessed, with the finding indicating that caregiving responsibilities negatively impacted relationships and emotional well-being. Caregivers of individuals with chronic low back pain reported reduced marital satisfaction and increased distress, particularly when perceived recipients’ disability levels were higher [ 74 ]. Two studies reported the impact of caregiving on physical disability and pain among caregivers of individuals with SCIs [ 84 , 85 ]. Quality of Life of Caregivers: Measurement Approaches and Key Findings Measurement Approaches and Instruments Quality of life among caregivers was assessed in 11 studies [ 32 , 57 , 66 , 69 , 75 , 79 , 83 , 85 , 86 , 93 , 94 ], using various instruments, including SF-36 [ 69 , 83 , 86 , 93 ], SF-12 [ 79 , 94 ], EQ-5D-5L [ 57 , 93 ], SF-8 [ 66 ], the World Health Organization Quality of Life-BREF Nepali Version [ 85 ], and the direct health utility elicitation method (i.e., standard gamble) [ 75 ]. Among studies employing QoL measures, two that applied the SF-36 and EQ-5D-5L reported caregivers' health status descriptively. Specifically, SF-36 results were presented as distributions across general health categories (e.g., Good, Fair, Poor) without reporting domain scores or summary measures [ 69 ]. Similarly, the EQ-5D-5L reported percentages of caregivers experiencing issues in each dimension (e.g., Mobility, Self-care, Usual Activities, Pain/Discomfort, Anxiety/Depression) without deriving an overall utility value [ 32 ]. Key Findings Caregivers’ health status varied widely across regions, with some reporting good health, while others reported poorer outcomes [ 57 , 69 ]. Some studies highlighted mental health challenges, particularly among caregivers of musculoskeletal injury and osteoporotic fractures [ 66 , 94 ]. For example, in Australia, caregivers had significantly lower mental health scores (MCS = 36.35) compared with the general population (MCS = 50) with a statistically significant decline observed over time ( p = 0.001). Moreover, greater caregiver resilience was positively associated with improved patient’s physical health ( β = 0.69, p = 0.003) [ 94 ]. Similarly, caregivers in Japan reported both physical and mental health scores significantly below the national average [ 66 ]. Caregivers of SCI individuals in Turkey and Iran also reported significantly lower QoL than controls, with the Iranian study using general population data and the Turkish study employing matched healthy controls [ 83 , 86 ]. Additionally, high-burden caregivers (ZBI score ≥24) reported significantly worse bodily pain and mental health than low-burden caregivers in the spinal muscular atrophy study conducted in Germany [ 93 ]. Economic Burden of Informal Caregiving Informal Care Hours: Measurement Approaches and Key Findings Measurement Approaches A total of 12 studies [ 32 , 35 , 56 – 58 , 66 , 67 , 84 , 85 , 90 , 93 , 101 ] reported on informal care hours using various data collection methods. Majority of studies used structured surveys [ 66 , 80 , 81 , 95 – 97 , 99 ], typically consisting of self-administered questionnaires completed online, by post, or in person. Others used interviewer-administered formats [ 72 , 78 , 85 , 98 ], where researchers recorded participants’ responses directly by phone or in person and established databases [ 73 , 88 – 91 ]. Except for one study [ 80 ], all other studies relied on a recall method to elicit data. Some studies disaggregated caregiving hours based on task type [ 32 , 56 , 57 , 72 , 73 , 81 , 90 , 95 ]. Two studies applied a cap on daily caregiving hours, limiting recorded time to a maximum of 16–17.2 h per day to reflect a typical waking day [ 90 , 99 ]. Key Findings Caregivers of individuals with MSCs report varying amounts of caregiving time depending on the condition and severity. Caregiving hours ranged widely, from a median of 1.16 h per day for osteoarthritis [ 56 ] to up to 19.3 h per day for multiple conditions such as osteoporosis, rheumatoid arthritis, and disk [ 58 ] (Table 2 ). An exploratory meta-analysis was conducted using six studies that provided informal care hours along with standard deviation [ 32 , 56 , 58 , 66 , 85 , 93 ]. Of these, one study reported informal care hours for both rheumatoid arthritis and osteoarthritis [ 56 ], resulting in a total of seven data points. The meta-analyzed informal care hours across six studies was 58.4 h per week (95% CI 21.08–95.82; I 2 = 99.92%) [Appendix 3 of the ESM]. Informal Care Costs: Valuation Methods and Key Findings Valuation Methods The most frequently employed approaches to measure informal care costs were the opportunity cost method [ 66 , 70 , 78 , 80 , 88 , 89 , 96 , 97 , 99 ], followed by the replacement cost method [ 81 , 90 , 95 , 98 ]. Two studies employed the contingent valuation method [ 73 , 90 ], while three studies used a combination of valuation methods [ 72 , 90 , 91 ] (Table 3 ). Valuation of informal care hours varied across and within cost approaches. The replacement cost method typically applied median wages for professional caregivers, with rates adjusted by task and sourced from national labor data or local wage agreements [ 81 , 95 , 98 ]. One study applied a standardized national rate for professional home-help services [ 90 ]. The opportunity cost method involved a range of wage assumptions, including 35% of full wages [ 80 ], national minimum wages, age-adjusted rates [ 88 , 96 ], and employment status [ 66 , 72 ]. After adjusting costs to 2023 US Dollars (USD), the unit cost of informal care hours ranged widely across studies, from $10.50 per hour in Canada [ 98 ] to over $64.25 per hour in the Netherlands [ 72 ] per hour, depending on the wage rate and valuation method. The mean unit costs were calculated at approximately $31.16 per hour for the opportunity cost method and $20.57 per hour for the replacement cost method, excluding studies that did not report specific wage (Table 3 ). Key Findings Detailed results of economic costs are presented in Table 3 . Among the 16 economic burden studies reviewed, 11 either explicitly reported or allowed the calculation of the share of informal care within total costs. Of these, eight were full COI studies, which considered formal healthcare costs, informal care, productivity losses, and other direct and indirect costs from a societal perspective, while three were partial COI studies with more limited scopes. In the full COI studies, the contribution of informal care to total costs ranged from 3% for a hip fracture in Canada [ 98 ] to 54.1% for rheumatoid arthritis in Italy [ 81 ]. Most studies reported figures between 30% and 41%, depending on disease severity, population characteristics, and methodological approach [ 70 , 88 , 95 , 96 ]. The three partial COI studies reported markedly higher shares of informal care: 66.4% of total post-fracture costs in the UK (including formal care, informal care, home adaptations, and physiotherapy) [ 99 ]; between 41.1% and 80% of societal costs for fibromyalgia in Spain, depending on the costing method used [ 90 ]; and 83% of non-medical costs for rheumatoid arthritis in Sweden [ 80 ] (Table 3 ). Studies revealed appreciable informal caregiving cost differences based on MSC type. For example, in a Spanish study focusing on fibromyalgia, informal care costs per recipient using the replacement cost method ranged from $61,827 (capped at 16 h/day) to $74,607 (uncapped), based on a 1-year time horizon [ 90 ]. Rheumatoid arthritis also imposes significant informal care costs, with an Italian study estimating annual expenses that ranged from $2358 for mild cases to $34,762 for severe cases using the replacement cost method over a 1-year period [ 81 ]. Similarly, in the Netherlands, weekly informal care costs for rheumatoid arthritis were estimated at $96.72 using the opportunity cost method and $351.72 using the replacement cost method [ 72 ]. Osteoporosis-related fractures presented a substantial economic burden, varying by country and fracture type. In Austria, the total annual informal care cost was estimated at $391.9 million [ 88 ], while in the UK, informal care for hip fractures during a 4-month recovery period ranged from $1,247.76 to $12,497 per person, depending on the methodology used [ 99 ]. In Canada, a 37-day recovery period led to an estimated caregiving cost of $79.53 million, based on approximately 9700 employed informal caregivers [ 89 ], while in Japan, weekly productivity losses averaged $476.94 per caregiver [ 66 ]. Other chronic MSCs, such as sarcopenia, also impose significant long-term financial strains. In the UK, the mean annual caregiving cost for sarcopenia was estimated at $2588 per caregiver using the opportunity cost method [ 96 ]. At the national level, fibromyalgia accounted for the highest informal care costs among MSCs, estimated at $7.27 billion using the replacement cost method (censored) in Spain [ 90 ]. This figure was based on approximately 275,841 adults with recognized fibromyalgia-related disability, 57% of whom reportedly received informal care, within an adult population of 40.8 million in 2021. Back pain followed, with estimated costs that ranged from $2.1 to $2.2 billion USD in the UK, depending on the valuation approach. These figures were derived from 1998 data, assuming a prevalence of 36–37% among 47.7 million adults (approximately 17.3 million individuals); however, the proportion of individuals with back pain receiving informal care was not specified [ 91 ]. Although the estimates have been standardized to 2023 USD, the substantial time gap between studies and differing health system contexts limit their direct comparability. Discussion This systematic review provides the first comprehensive synthesis of the psychological and economic burden of informal caregiving for MSCs. Our findings indicate a substantial impact on caregivers’ mental health, productivity, and QoL. Beyond overall burden assessments, we identified significant effects on pain, stress, anxiety, and depression, highlighting the multidimensional nature of caregiving. The psychological burden on caregivers of individuals with MSCs varies across condition types and burden domains. In the reviewed studies, ZBI scores ranged from 18.4 to 42, indicating mild-to-moderate levels [ 66 , 79 ]. Some studies also assessed caregivers’ QoL alongside the burden [ 66 , 69 ]. While the 22-item ZBI is widely used, its ordinal structure complicates interpretation and cross-study comparison (e.g., score ranges: 0–21 = little or no burden; 21–40 = mild-to-moderate burden; 41–60 = moderate-to-severe burden; 61–88 = severe burden) [ 102 ]. Combining ZBI with QoL instruments offers a more nuanced and interpretable assessment, which can improve comparability and help identify caregivers at risk of severe burden, informing more targeted interventions. Time-related burden consistently emerged as the most prominent caregiving domain across studies. The CBI identified time-dependent burden as the highest in all cases [ 58 , 59 , 67 , 68 , 100 ], while the CRA highlighted disrupted schedules as one of the most significant sources of strain [ 32 , 56 , 57 ]. An exploratory synthesis of studies reporting informal care hours also indicated substantial weekly time demands; however, the small number of studies and considerable heterogeneity limit the generalizability of these findings to all MSCs. Despite this, the convergence of evidence across individual studies reinforces the central role of time burden in shaping caregiver experiences. The prolonged duration of care [ 32 , 56 , 101 ], coupled with the high intensity of daily caregiving activities [ 34 , 36 , 90 ], amplifies this strain, highlighting the need for sustained support mechanisms such as financial aid and respite care. Caregivers of PwMSC frequently experience significant psychological strain, as evidenced by elevated scores on various instruments [ 57 , 74 , 101 ], with poorer mental health outcomes closely associated with higher burden levels [ 57 , 93 ]. The well-being of caregivers was found to be significantly correlated with well-being of the PwMSC [ 74 , 85 , 100 ], highlighting the need for a holistic approach to care that supports both individuals with MSCs and caregivers. Interventions aimed at improving pain management [ 103 ] or rehabilitation [ 104 ] could indirectly benefit caregivers’ mental health and QoL. The impact of caregiving for MSCs on health-related QoL was evident in most studies, with caregivers often experiencing significant declines in physical, mental, and social well-being [ 66 , 75 , 83 , 86 , 94 , 101 ]. Declines in health-related QoL were more pronounced among caregivers experiencing high burden or caring for individuals with more severe conditions [ 57 , 93 ]. These findings stress the need for targeted mental health support and social policy responses that address the broader dimensions of caregiver well-being [ 67 , 79 , 86 , 93 ]. The physical burden of caregiving for individuals with MSCs is evident in our review, where caregivers reported significant pain and disability, as seen in studies measuring pain intensity and disability [ 84 , 85 ]. This finding is further supported by health-related QoL assessments, which show lower physical functioning scores, including mobility issues [ 32 , 83 , 86 , 101 ]. In addition to these burdens, some studies also acknowledged positive caregiving experiences. Caregivers of individuals with arthritis reported high self-esteem, illustrating that caregiving can also provide a sense of fulfillment [ 32 , 56 , 57 ]. These findings suggest that tools like the CRA are effective in capturing both the burdens and rewards of caregiving. Further research should explore these positive dimensions across different MSCs and cultural contexts to better understand the full scope of caregiving experiences. Our systematic review highlights the substantial economic burden of informal caregiving for MSCs, shaped by geographic region, valuation methods, and disease severity. Over a 1-year time horizon, informal caregiving [ 91 ] costs per PwMSC ranged widely from approximately $1700 USD for post-hip fracture care in Canada (including acute hospitalization, rehabilitation, long-term care, and home-based informal support) [ 98 ], to over $74,600 USD for chronic fibromyalgia cases in Spain [ 90 ]. Intensive caregiving periods following musculoskeletal events, such as fractures, also contribute substantially to informal care costs [ 70 , 89 , 99 ]. At the national level, informal care costs ranged from hundreds of millions to nearly $7.3 billion USD, including estimates for osteoporosis in Austria [ 88 ], fibromyalgia in Spain [ 90 ], and back pain in the UK [ 91 ]. These findings emphasize the economic strain MSCs impose not only on families but also on broader health systems, particularly where formal care services are lacking. The cost estimates of informal caregiving vary widely because of differences in costing methods, assumptions, and the lack of methodological consistency across studies. This was clearly demonstrated in studies from the Netherlands and Spain, where the replacement cost method yielded the highest estimates, and in the Spanish study, willingness to accept -based estimates were notably higher than willingness to pay [ 72 , 90 ]. Combining valuation approaches, as done in studies from the Netherlands, UK, and Spain [ 72 , 90 , 91 ], provides a more comprehensive assessment of the economic value of informal care. Sensitivity analyses from the UK, Spain, and Canada illustrate how cost estimates shift significantly based on assumptions like wage rates or caregiving hour limits [ 90 , 98 , 99 ]. Subgroup analyses also reveal variation in costs based on factors such as disease severity [ 81 , 90 ] and patient demographics [ 78 ]. These variations highlight the need for consistent, severity-adjusted valuation methods to improve comparability and inform policy more effectively. Despite various methodological efforts, most studies relied solely on economic proxies such as time input and wage value. Only two studies in this review applied preference-based methods [ 73 , 90 ] to capture caregivers’ personal valuations. Their limited use presents an opportunity for future research to adopt more individualized, caregiver-centered approaches to cost estimation [ 105 ]. This review also identified several limitations in assessing the burden of informal caregiving for MSCs. These include the lack of data on disease severity, caregiving duration, and disease progression, as well as inconsistent reporting of task-specific care and incomplete utility data. Methodological heterogeneity in data collection and valuation approaches further limited cross-study comparability. Future research should adopt standardized instruments for assessing psychological burden, such as the ZBI or CBI. These well-validated tools capture multiple dimensions of caregiver strain. The CRA may also be valuable when both negative and positive aspects of caregiving, such as caregiver esteem or perceptions of family support, are of interest. In addition, caregiving time should be reported by task and stratified by disease severity to improve consistency in time valuation. To enhance future economic evaluations, researchers should better combine opportunity cost and replacement cost approaches using standardized and transparent assumptions such as clearly defined time inputs, caregiver tasks, and disease severity levels. This is especially important given the wide variability in cost estimates resulting from methodological differences. Crucially, preference-based methods, such as discrete choice experiments, should be more widely adopted. These approaches go beyond economic proxies by capturing the subjective value caregivers place on their contributions, reflecting their lived experiences, priorities, and well-being. Incorporating these perspectives can generate more meaningful, caregiver-centered evidence to inform policy and support programs [ 18 , 106 – 109 ]. Strengths and Limitations of this Review A key strength of this review is its dual focus on both the economic and psychological burden of informal caregiving in MSCs, offering a more comprehensive understanding of caregiver experiences. The review was guided by a systematic search strategy, with screening and data extraction processes conducted independently by multiple reviewers to reduce selection bias. In addition, this study captured a wide range of MSCs and caregiver outcomes, increasing its relevance for both health and policy audiences. Several limitations should also be acknowledged. First, the review was limited to studies published in English, potentially introducing language bias and omitting relevant data from non-English literature. Gray literature was not included, which may have contributed to publication bias. An exploratory meta-analysis was conducted for informal care hours; however, because of the small number of studies and high heterogeneity, the findings are not generalizable. Economic and psychological outcomes were synthesized narratively because of the substantial variation in study designs, outcome measures, and valuation methods, which limit the precision and comparability of the overall burden estimates. Finally, although the risk of bias was assessed using the EVERS and CASP checklists, the methodological quality of included studies varied, which may influence the interpretation of some findings. In particular, the lack of standardized assessment tools and valuation frameworks across studies complicates efforts to synthesize findings and draw generalizable conclusions about caregiver burden in MSCs. Conclusions This systematic review is the first to synthesize the psychological and economic burdens of informal caregiving specifically for MSCs. While burdens such as stress, depression, and economic strain are broadly acknowledged in the caregiving literature, this review clarifies how these challenges manifest in the MSC context and highlights the methodological fragmentation that hinders meaningful comparison across studies. Informal caregivers of individuals with MSCs experience considerable psychological distress, physical strain, and opportunity costs, with wide variability in caregiving hours and costs depending on disease severity, valuation method, and geographic context. However, inconsistencies in study design, outcome measures, and economic valuation frameworks limit the comparability of findings. Standardizing assessment tools and valuation methods is essential to generate more robust evidence and inform effective policies. In parallel, structured support systems including financial compensation, psychological interventions, and workplace accommodations are needed to reduce caregiver burden and promote caregiver well-being. documents.title: The clinical effect and safety of non-pharmacological Chinese medicine therapy in treating chronic nonspecific low back pain: a systematic review and network meta-analysis protocol.
documents.abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Chronic nonspecific low back pain (CNLBP) significantly affects individual wellbeing, compromising physical health, quality of life, and productivity. As healthcare approaches expand, Non-pharmacological Chinese Medicine Therapies (NPCMT) have garnered global interest. This systematic review and network meta-analysis (NMA) aims to rigorously evaluate the effectiveness and prioritization of various NPCMT interventions for CNLBP, including acupuncture, tui na, gua sha, cupping therapy, taijiquan, baduanjin, yijinjing, and qigong, ultimately providing evidence-based recommendations for healthcare professionals.
METHODS AND ANALYSIS: Our strategy encompasses a meticulous hunt for randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that evaluate Non-pharmacological Chinese Medicine Therapies for treating chronic nonspecific low back pain. This exploration will span an array of databases, such as Web of Science, Cochrane Library, EMBASE, PubMed, China National Knowledge Infrastructure, China Science and Technology Journal Database, Wanfang Database, China Biology Medicine disc, and ClinicalTrials.gov. Our examination will be comprehensive, encompassing evaluations of risk of bias, meta-analytic procedures, analyses of subgroups and sensitivity, assessments concerning publication bias, and the determination of the quality of evidence.
CONCLUSION: This study aims to offer valuable insights into the safety and efficacy of various Non-pharmacological Chinese Medicine therapies for patients with CNLBP. It is hoped that these findings will guide future clinical practice and research in identifying the most suitable treatment methods for CNLBP patients.
documents.conclusions: This study aims to offer valuable insights into the safety and efficacy of various Non-pharmacological Chinese Medicine therapies for patients with CNLBP. It is hoped that these findings will guide future clinical practice and research in identifying the most suitable treatment methods for CNLBP patients.

This exploration will span an array of databases, such as Web of Science, Cochrane Library, EMBASE, PubMed, China National Knowledge Infrastructure, China Science and Technology Journal Database, Wanfang Database, China Biology Medicine disc, and ClinicalTrials.gov .
